searchResults.name: Rattlesnake Ledge Trail
searchResults.description: Located only a short 30 minute drive from downtown Bellevue and less than an hour away from Seattle, the climb up to the Rattlesnake Ledges is a very popular hiking trail in the summer months. Not only does this trail provide great panoramic views from atop Rattlesnake Ridge, but there is also a great park located below. Many people come to enjoy the lake in the warmer months. There are no motorboats or fishing allowed on the lake, making it an ideal destination for kayakers and...

searchResults.name: Wallace Falls via Woody Trail
searchResults.description:
Located roughly an hour from Seattle, Wallace Falls makes for a great family-friendly day hike. The route is scenic the whole way, as the Woody Trail meanders along the Wallace River, through lush vegetation. Don’t let the elevation gain scare you, much of it occurs later in the hike, between the Middle and Upper Falls. You can go as far as you like before turning around.

The hike is very popular, so it’s best to get there early, especially on weekends. There are bathrooms and water...

searchResults.area_name: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Chirico Trail to Poo-Poo Point
searchResults.location_label: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: The Chirico Trail is a lovely spot conveniently located just off I-90 in Issaquah. After about 700 feet of elevation gain, the noise from any roads nearly disappears, and nothing but forest remains. The south launching pad area allows you to have lovely valley views while looking out over the top of the nudist colony. The north launch area of Poo-Poo Point allows you to have lovely views of Lake Sammamish and Issaquah. This trail is a great way to watch hang gliders, paragliders, and other...

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Mount Si Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description:
The Mount Si Trail is one of the most popular trails in Washington, and for good reason. Less than an hour from Seattle, the summit offers incredible views of the Snoqualmie River Valley and the surrounding area.

There is a very large parking area at the trailhead, but it does fill up on warm weekends. Per usual, it’s best to arrive early. A Discover Pass is required.

The hike is hard enough to be a challenge, but not so difficult that weekend warriors can’t climb it. The trail is almost...

searchResults.name: Twin Falls Trail
searchResults.description:
The Twin Falls Trail is a lovely hike, weaving through lush vegetation, eventually reaching a series of large waterfalls. With its moderate difficulty, and ease of access from I-90, this trail is great for families.

Twin Falls can be accessed via the Twin Falls Trailhead off of Exit 34, or from the east via the Homestead Valley Trailhead (Exit 38). Most people choose the mapped route on this page, the Twin Falls Trailhead.

The route sets out eastward along the South Fork Snoqualmie River....

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Little Si Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description:
Little Si is the little sister to Mount Si. The trail is easier with less elevation, but the view from the top is just as breathtaking with views of Snoqualmie Valley and Rattlesnake Mountain. The trail is often covered in snow and difficult to trek through much of the year and many hikers suggest this as a summer hike.

The beginning section is the steepest part, so don’t get disheartened! The trail is well-traveled and marked with signs. You will likely see rock climbers along the...

searchResults.name: Mount Storm King
searchResults.description:
Mount Storm King is one of the most popular trails at Lake Crescent. Even with its popularity, it does come with some serious considerations before hiking. 

The trail climbs steeply for the first 2 miles to an "End of Maintained Trail" sign. Olympic National Park does not maintain the trail above this point. 
The last 1/4 mile involves a steep rocky trail with a series of ropes. These ropes can only be used by one person at a time and help hikers ascend and descend this steeper section. The...

searchResults.name: Lake 22 Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
Lake Twenty-Two Trail is a beautiful hike to an alpine lake through old-growth forests ending with stunning mountain views of Mount Pilchuck. The trail can be accessed off of Mountain Loop Highway in the North Cascades area of Washington. The trailhead is located east of Granite Falls. 

The path starts out gently enough on a dirt staircase through lush rainforest. You will hear flowing water from Twenty-Two Creek along the way. A bridge crosses the creek around a mile in where there is a...

searchResults.name: Marymere Falls Trail
searchResults.description:
The Marymere Falls Trail is a short hike through wonderful Pacific Northwest scenery from Lake Crescent, through large towering trees, and encompassing incredible river views. It is one of the most popular trails in Olympic National Park. The trail begins by the Storm King Ranger Station and features a nice gentle rise in elevation up to the falls and a pleasant descent. It's a great family-friendly outing in an old-growth forest. 

Lush greenery and beautiful waterways abound on this short...

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Teneriffe Falls Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: This is a steep and challenging trail to a beautiful waterfall. The trail is very steep and rocky towards the end, sturdy footwear and trekking poles are recommended. The best time to visit the falls is during the spring or after heavy rain when the falls are flowing the strongest. Snow and ice is common on the trail in the winter.

searchResults.area_name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Dirty Harry's Balcony via Birdhouse Trail
searchResults.location_label: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: This is a great option for those looking for a quick escape from the city. Just a short drive from Seattle, Dirty Harry's Balcony has incredible views of the valley and nearby mountain peaks. For a relatively short hike compared to other trails in the area, the payoff at the end of this trail is well worth the effort.

searchResults.area_name: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Poo Poo Point Trail
searchResults.location_label: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description:
Poo Poo Point Trail is a popular destination in the Tiger Mountain State Forest, located in the Issaquah Alps. On the shoulder of West Tiger Mountain, this trail reaches heights that come with great views of Mount Rainier, particularly at sunset! The point is a popular launching pad for paragliders and hang gliders. It is also a perfect spot for a picnic at one of the many picnic tables. 

Note that the mapped route on this page is not the most popular approach to Poo Poo Point. This route...

searchResults.name: Heybrook Lookout Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This is a short but steep climb offering stunning views from the top of a fire tower that has been on the top of the hill since 1925. Access to the top of the tower is not always open. The trail begins by traveling through a dense wooded forest filled with ferns and moss before arriving at the base of the tower. The area is very popular, so an early start on weekends is recommended.

searchResults.name: Cherry Creek Falls Trail
searchResults.description:
All visitor vehicles must park off the county road (Mountain View Road). Any cars parked on the road will be ticketed and towed by the King County Sheriffs Department as the roadway needs to remain clear for emergency vehicles to pass. 

The start of the hike is on private property. When passing through private property easements and right-of-ways it is especially important to stay on the path and respect posted guidance. Local officials and private landowners work in partnership to provide...

searchResults.name: Bridal Veil Falls and Lunch Rock via Lake Serene Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
Lake Serene is an alpine lake nestled in the Cascade mountains of Washington State. Lake Serene Trail is a popular hike within the Mount Baker Snoqualamie Forest. The trailhead can be accessed off of Mount Index Road near Stevens Pass. Make sure to get an early start in order to get a parking spot at the trailhead.

What the trail lacks in length, it makes up for in elevation gain. The first mile and a half winds across a well manicured and slightly inclined path, at the end of which you can...

searchResults.area_name: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area
searchResults.name: West Tiger #3
searchResults.location_label: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: The West Tiger #3 Trail is a gradual climb up, and then gets steeper in the last half mile leading towards the summit. During a clear day there are views of Seattle and Mount Rainier. Leading up to this point you will be in a dense forest with a moss and fern covered forest floor. The colors are beautiful in the fall.

searchResults.name: Discovery Park and Lighthouse Loop
searchResults.description:
The park provides an open space away from the stress and activity of the city, a sanctuary for wildlife, and an outdoor classroom for people to learn about the natural world. The park is also home to the Daybreak Star Indian Cultural Center.

Discovery Park is a 534 acre natural area park, located next to the peninsular Magnolia neighborhood in Seattle, and overlooking Puget Sound, with views of the Cascade and Olympic mountains. The park includes two miles of protected tidal beaches, a...

searchResults.name: Margaret's Way Trail to Debbie's View
searchResults.description:
Beginning from the Squak Mountain Lodge, the trail heads through the parking and camping area using old access and logging roads before becoming a true trail. Roads once laced the upper reaches of the mountain, but these are now mostly overgrown with moss-laden bigleaf maple, cedar, western hemlock, and a few Douglas-fir, thanks in part to MacLeod's work to preserve this area. 

Once you step onto the trail itself, you'll wind your way along a hillside, continuing on a moderate grade through...

searchResults.name: Snoqualmie Falls Trail
searchResults.description:
Snoqualmie Falls is a legendary scenic attraction known for its striking beauty and for being featured in cameo roles on many movies and TV shows. Fans of the cult classic "Twin Peaks" may recognize the falls as the filming location for the show's opening credits. These breathtaking falls draw in many visitors, so be prepared for crowds on this short trail, especially on summer weekend days. 

All in all, this route is a family favorite in Washington and should not be missed.

Accessibility: ...

searchResults.name: Coal Creek Falls Loop via Red Town and Cave Hole Trail
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description:
This enjoyable trail to a beautiful waterfall can get muddy at times. It has a little bit of everything: river, falls, and meadow. 

You can ride your horse on a portion of this loop, but not down all the way to the falls. Horseback riding is allowed on the Red Town, Quarry, and Cave Hole trails, but not on the Coal Creek Falls section. For more information on equestrian-friendly trails in the park, visit: https://aqua.kingcounty.gov/gis/web/VMC/recreation/BCT_CougarMtn_brochure.pdf

searchResults.area_name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Mailbox Peak Trail Loop
searchResults.location_label: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description:
Mailbox Peak Loop is a challenging hike in the North Bend area that combines the Old Trail with the New Trail created by the Department of Natural Resources.

The Old Trail is very challenging with sharp inclines all the way up through the forest. The trail was easy to follow until about 3000 feet where it gets covered by falling pines and leaves. Luckily the White Diamond Trail markers are well placed and easy to follow. Once the Old Trail meets the New Trail it's pretty straightforward from...

searchResults.name: Heather Lake Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Heather Lake Trail is a great day hike with a decent amount of elevation gain, which provides panoramic views of Mount Philchuck. The trail travels through the forest and lollipops around Heather Lake. There are lots of places here that are perfect for a break or a picnic. This area is home to abundant wildlife and wildflowers during the spring months. The Heather Lake trail is known for its many tree roots and rocky sections, which can be slippery, especially after rain. Be prepared for a...

searchResults.name: Lower Lena Lake Trail
searchResults.description: This is a nice trail in Olympic National Forest with a moderate climb up to Lake Lena. Dogs are allowed but cannot go on the trail to Upper Lake Lena, as it is part of Olympic National Park, and dogs are not allowed on trails in the national park. Expect company as it is a very popular trail. You will need a recreation pass to park at the trailhead.

searchResults.name: Little Mashel Falls Trail via Bud Blancher Trail
searchResults.location_label: Charles Lathrop Pack Experimental Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Middle Mashel Falls is the main attraction, so if time is crunched, skip the Upper Falls. There are lots of wild blackberries along the trail during the right season. The trail is steep in sections and can get slippery. Trekking poles and sturdy footwear are recommended. There is plenty of beautiful scenery along the way. The path is known to be poorly marked with many confusing splits. To ensure you find the 125-foot Middle Falls and for your overall safety, make sure you download the route...

searchResults.name: Bridal Veil Falls Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Bridal Veil Falls is a beautiful waterfall that roars down a 100-foot rock face, sliding off of granite slabs and tumbling onto the rocks and Bridal Veil Creek down below. The majority of elevation gain is on the Bridal Veil trail turnoff about 1/2 mile from the top. Here, you will also climb flights of stairs to get to the top. There is a lot of skree around this point of the hike, but you are rewarded with a stunning view in both directions once you’re there. Bring layers, as there are...

searchResults.area_name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Mailbox Peak (Old) Trail
searchResults.location_label: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: The old Mailbox Peak Trail is a steep trail leading from the Mailbox Peak Trailhead to the summit. It is unforgiving, there are no switchbacks to be found. It is mostly wooded until around the 2-mile mark where things open up and there are views of the surrounding mountains. The upper parking lot is usually closed during the winter months, so plan accordingly and arrive early. Because the old trail can be hard to follow through the rooted sections, it's smart to download the route before you...

searchResults.name: Little Mashel Falls via 1000, 1070 Road and Little Mashel Falls Trail
searchResults.location_label: Charles Lathrop Pack Experimental Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
The trail passes by three waterfalls: two medium-sized and one very large, with a 125-foot drop. Access can be challenging but is definitely worthwhile.

The largest waterfall in the gorge, on the Little Mashel River, flows over a small punchbowl, then slides down a smooth concave lip before plunging 125 feet onto large boulders below. If you visit during spring when the river is at its peak, you'll see a stunning wall of water and spray. In late summer, the falls become calmer and more...

searchResults.name: Pinnacle Peak Loop
searchResults.description: This trail can be steep in some areas but there are plenty of places to stop and catch your breath. There is a view of Rainier but not from the lookout. The viewpoint is just off the main trail. The trail can be hiked in either direction - so choose if you would rather have the steep uphill or the steep descent. Nice big parking lot with bathrooms. The trail is well-maintained. Bring plenty of water. Because the loop has a number of intersecting paths and can be hard to follow, it is a great...

searchResults.name: Point Defiance Park Outer Loop
searchResults.description:
This well-marked and gentle loop through Point Defiance Park is a great option for the whole family. You'll pass by several incredible viewpoints of Puget Sound, the historic Fort Nisqually, and several great spots to stop for a picnic. If time allows, check out the zoo and aquarium near the parking lot at the start. After rainstorms, the trail may be muddy, and roots and rocks may be exposed.

Parks Tacoma maintains this trail.

Visitors using wheelchairs, mobility...

searchResults.name: Icicle Ridge Trail Overlook
searchResults.description:
The entire Icicle Ridge Trail provides access to Alpine Lakes Wilderness. The first 3 miles of this trail provide a good day hike, climbing quickly from Icicle Ridge Trailhead to the ridge line and offering views into the Lower Icicle Creek Valley. This is the most popular section of the trail.

This trail provides access to Alpine Lakes Wilderness.

searchResults.name: Green Mountain Lookout via Gold Creek Trail
searchResults.description:
A moderate climb to great views of the Olympics, Bremerton, and even Mount Rainier. Look for a seasonal waterfall on your left in the beginning.

Heads up! It's a good chance that you'll be sharing the trail with other hikers, bikers, dogs, and horses. Keep an eye out for others on the trail and remember general trail etiquette: horses and uphill traffic have the right of way, and dogs should yield to everyone else on the trail.

searchResults.name: Lime Kiln Trail
searchResults.location_label: Robe Canyon Historic Trail Park, Washington
searchResults.description: This is a lovely forested walk alongside a river. The trail is often lush and green with trees, ferns, and other foliage. There are some points on this trail it is important to watch your step and keep a close eye on young children, as there are drop-offs and a slippery log bridge.  If you take the river loop, and the water is low enough there is a nice beach to rest at. This trail can sometimes be overgrown and muddy, so long pants and sturdy footwear is recommended.

searchResults.name: Green Lake Trail
searchResults.description:
Inside one of Seattle's most beloved parks, this paved path loops around Green Lake.

Geologists say the Vashon Glacial Ice Sheet, which also formed Puget Sound and other area lakes, formed Green Lake 50,000 years ago. Dredgings of Green Lake have produced volcanic ash from an eruption of Glacier Peak that occurred about 6,700 years ago.

The lake was included in the Olmsted Brothers' comprehensive parks plan and was given to the City by the State of Washington in 1905. Green Lake underwent a...

searchResults.name: Devil's Punchbowl via Spruce Railroad Trail
searchResults.description:
The trek to the Devil’s Punchbowl will take you along the shoreline of Lake Crescent for a little over a mile. At this point, you will see the first old train tunnel. It is about 75 yards long and can get dark in the middle. If you enter the tunnel, a flashlight and reflective gear can be helpful. 

To get to the Devil’s Punchbowl as routed, you will split off from the paved trail and turn left just before the train tunnel to take a short, unpaved side trail to the punchbowl. 

The Devil’s...

searchResults.name: Longview Peak and Far Country Lookout Loop
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description: This loop starts and ends at the Sky Country trailhead via several trails in the central part of Cougar Mountain. First, you will hike up to Shy Bear Pass, then head towards the Doughty Falls Viewpoint. Coal Creek Falls is also along the loop. The falls are best viewed during the spring; by late summer, they often dry up. There are several connecting trails, so it is recommended to download the route beforehand.

searchResults.name: Upper Big Creek Loop
searchResults.description: This hike is well worth the journey up through the gorgeous cedars and conifers to the falls and fast flowing creek. The trail is well-marked and well-maintained. Go clockwise and plan on taking advantage of the benches and boulders for rest breaks as the climb gets a bit more challenging. Trekking poles are recommended.

searchResults.area_name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Granite Lakes Trail
searchResults.location_label: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: This trail ascends through a valley surrounded by mountain peaks to two pristine alpine lakes. The trail is well-maintained but can be overgrown in some sections. Wearing pants is recommended. The lakes are a great spot to take a swim, stop for a snack break and take in the scenery. Bring bug spray in the early summer.

searchResults.name: Mount Walker
searchResults.description: There are two ways to get to the top of Mount Walker. You can either hike, as shown on this page or drive to the top. This hike is short, yet steep, and takes you to the north and south viewpoints. It then returns down the same trail. From the top, enjoy panoramic views of the surrounding mountains, including those of Olympic National Park, as well as the looking across the water towards Seattle and other cities.

searchResults.name: Soundview and Grandview Loop
searchResults.description:
This family-friendly trail goes around the Chambers Bay Golf Course and has great views of the Puget Sound. This trail is ranked moderate and not easy because it includes steep rolling hills.

Accessibility: There are 4 designated accessible spaces in the paved parking lot off of Grandview Drive West at the southeast end of the trail. All of them are van-accessible with striped access aisles. The trail surface is paved asphalt and smooth. It is typically at least 6 feet wide.

The most...

searchResults.name: Hole-in-the-Wall from Rialto Beach
searchResults.description:
This hike begins at Rialto Beach and goes north 1.5 miles to Split Rock and Hole-in-the-Wall. There is no trail, since you will be hiking on the beach itself. 

The most important thing to consider is the tide level. Tides change every day and typically have 2 high tides and 2 low tides per day. Ideally, you are doing this hike at low tide. The maximum tide height you should consider this hike is around 6 feet. Otherwise, the ocean water will cover the beach and you will have nowhere to...

searchResults.name: Mount Washington Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: The best route off the interstate is to take exit 38 to reach the trailhead. The trail climbs through the forest and passes a steep rocky outcropping about a half mile from the trailhead. This spot is popular with rock climbers and you may notice climbing hardware hanging from the cliff. As you ascend you are rewarded with some views, the summit has a perfect view of Mt. Rainier.

searchResults.name: Meadowdale Beach Park
searchResults.description:
This short, popular trail is ideal for families, or those just looking for a pleasant jaunt. Hikers pass through about a mile of beautiful forest, before popping out at the beach. This is a nice area to explore and take in the views. Save some energy for the way back, the climb from the beach can be tough!

Parking can be difficult here, there's a small parking lot at the trailhead that gets full early.

searchResults.name: Sequalitchew Creek Trail
searchResults.description:
This is an easy-to-follow and dog-friendly trail. The trail passes by old train tracks and briefly through a tunnel just before ending at the beach. The trail starts out by leaving the parking lot by City Hall and follows an old gravel road to Puget Sound. The trail then turns to pavement for a short section before returning to gravel. 

The City of DuPont maintains this trail.

Visitors using wheelchairs, mobility equipment, or strollers may need all-terrain tires...

searchResults.name: Dickerson Falls
searchResults.description: As a private landowner, Ueland Tree Farm reserves its rights to restrict or limit entry to its property. Exceptions to the below rules must be approved in writing in advance. When passing through private property easements and right-of-ways it is especially important to stay on the path and respect posted guidance. Local officials and private landowners work in partnership to provide public access to this area. Staying on the path while on private property ensures that agreements between...

searchResults.name: Lighthouse Point and Lottie Point via Rosario Head Trail
searchResults.description: This route explores a beautiful stretch of the Washington coast. You will first hike out onto a peninsula known as Rosario Head before walking along Bowman Bay. There is a nice sandy beach here and a picnic area. There are more stunning views of the rugged coast from Lighthouse and Lottie Point. Otters and seals can often be spotted in the water. Downloading offline maps is recommended.

searchResults.name: Nisqually Estuary Boardwalk and Twin Barns Trail
searchResults.description:
This gorgeous and easy walk takes visitors through diverse habitats, winding through tree groves, salt marshes, and a tidal river.  Please be aware that tidal changes will affect visitors' ability to spot wildlife. Boards may be slippery after there has been rain. Bring your binoculars, hat, and water.

Accessibility: This trail is likely accessible for visitors using wheelchairs, mobility equipment, or strollers. There are 4 designated van-accessible parking spaces with striped access aisles...

searchResults.area_name: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Cable Line Trail to West Tiger #3
searchResults.location_label: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: This is a steep, direct route from the road alongside I-90 to the top of West Tiger #3. The trail is wooded until you reach the summit which has been logged. From the summit, there are views of Mount Rainier and other surrounding mountains and lakes. There is a bench at the top to relax before heading back down.

searchResults.name: Cape Flattery Trail
searchResults.description:
Known for its sunsets, Cape Flattery is a nature sanctuary on the northwestern-most point in the continental United States where the Strait of Juan de Fuca meets the Pacific where sea meets dramatic headlands, sea stacks, and deep narrow coves.  View seabirds, whales and sea lions too.

Preserved by the Makah Indian Nation, the well-maintained trail leads through wet areas, along coastal cliffs and across boardwalks. Start through a mist-drenched forest of Sitka spruce. Utilizing boardwalks...

searchResults.name: Ebey's Landing Trail
searchResults.location_label: Ebey's Landing National Historical Reserve, Washington
searchResults.description:
The trail starts at the parking lot on Ebey's Landing Road. Continue on the Bluff Trail, then take a right, which takes you to the historic Sunnyside Cemetery. Then return to the Bluff Trail and continue around the loop down to the beach, and eventually back to your car.

Alternatively, you could start at the cemetery, completing the loop from there. It is important to research the tides before heading out on this trail, as the trail can only be completed as mapped during low tide.

searchResults.name: Whittaker Wilderness Peak Trail
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description:
This hike is similar to other Cougar Mountain hikes, semi-steep start with gentle trails once you reach the top of the park. This is the highest point within the Cougar Mountain Park. To get here you can take either the Wilderness Creek Trail or the Wilderness Cliffs Trail. The hike up to this point can be a challenge where you will encounter a steep climb and at times, rocky terrain. The final stretch to the peak is a gentle short climb where you can rest and relax. 

On your way up towards...

searchResults.name: Hall of Mosses Trail
searchResults.description: The Hall of Mosses is a primary example of a temperate rainforest ecosystem, defined by its immense scale and ancient growth. As you walk the loop, you will see "nurse logs"—fallen trees that serve as a biological foundation for new life. You can identify these by looking for rows of young saplings growing in a perfectly straight line atop a decaying trunk. This landscape is the traditional territory of the Hoh Tribe, who refer to the nearby river as Cha’lak’at’sit. For generations, the tribe...

searchResults.area_name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Mailbox Peak Trail
searchResults.location_label: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: Mailbox Peak Trail takes you to the summit of Mailbox Peak and offers beautiful panoramic views of the area. This route follows the new trail that was created by the Department of Natural Resources. The view at the top is breathtaking, especially on a clear day, with views of Mount Rainier and the Middle Fork Valley below. To return, take the New Mailbox Peak Trail back down to the parking area. The summit is steep and rocky, so make sure you come prepared with proper equipment. Microspikes...

searchResults.name: Spruce Nature Trail
searchResults.description: A short rainforest loop, the Spruce Nature Trail packs incredible variety into just a little over a mile. This is a great place to look for the fascinating phenomenon known as "nurse logs" - fallen trees which provide a place for new seedlings to grow. You can see them at every stage, from the new-fallen log with brand new baby trees sprouting on it to the rows of centuries-old trees whose "nurse log" has long since rotted away, leaving them standing in a perfectly straight line, called a...

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Mount Si via Old Si Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: Mount Si Trail is a very popular destination, and for good reason: it's less than an hour from Seattle, and the summit offers incredible views of the Snoqualmie River Valley and the surrounding area. This trail takes you up the old trail, which is less popular than the standard Mount Si Trail nearby. This is a challenging trail and trekking poles are recommended to navigate the steep and rocky terrain. From the top, you are rewarded with beautiful panoramic views. Hike this trail on a clear...

searchResults.name: Mima Falls East Trail
searchResults.description:
This Mima Falls Trail connects to other trails in the area which may not be well marked. Be sure to stay on the route in the map or have a map handy along the way.

Mima Falls is one of the highlights of the many trails that make up the expansive Capitol State Forest.  The hike is mostly easy, though you will pass through many muddy sections. It takes you through both old and new as well as cleared forests.  Mima Falls is a nice little 25 foot falls worth checking out.

Mima Falls takes its...

searchResults.name: Annette Lake Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
This trail is well-maintained, features a gentle but steady incline, and has a lot of varying scenery. The first portion of the trail can be muddy alongside waterfalls to get to the Annette Lake trailhead. A series of switchbacks through an old-growth forest make for a fun climb with beautiful views and stunning avalanche chutes.

In the winter months, bringing special equipment such as spikes or waterproof shoes is recommended. It’s a beautiful winter wonderland with lots of snowpacks in...

searchResults.name: Heybrook Ridge via Leovy Trail
searchResults.description:
The Leovy Trail begins near the Skykomish River and travels uphill to the Bridal Falls Viewpoint. There are great views of the surrounding mountains from this point. The trail is mostly wooded up until this point.

This trail can receive significant snowfall, so snowshoes are recommended during the winter season.

searchResults.name: Lake Washington Watertower, South Ridge, Beach and North Trail Loop
searchResults.description: This is a well-maintained trail through a wooded area with lake views right in the middle of the city. This loop can be hiked in either direction, but keep in mind it may be more challenging in the counter-clockwise direction. The trail can get muddy during the rainy season. Wear sturdy footwear and bring plenty of layers.

searchResults.name: Cedar Butte Trail
searchResults.description:
Hikers must either walk or ride a bike to trailheads. Please check the park page for up to date trail accessibility before visiting. 

This moderate hike has some steep spots, but offers stunning views from the top.

searchResults.name: Boulder River Trail
searchResults.description:
The Boulder River Trail leads to an unnamed waterfall, a feature that may be considered notable for its height and beauty. The trail itself offers a relatively easy path, but reaching the base of the falls involves a section that requires navigating steeper terrain. 

Those planning to visit should note that the route to the trailhead may be challenging; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended for navigating the road. The trail allows for an experience of natural beauty, culminating in views...

searchResults.name: Cave Hole, Coal Creek Falls, Quarry, and Fred's Railroad Loop
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description: Beautiful loop through a lush forest. There is plenty of shade along the way, making this trail a perfect place to escape the summer heat. This trail is very popular, and the parking lot can fill up. It is recommended to arrive early or come during the week. The trail can be muddy after a storm, so sturdy footwear is recommended.

searchResults.name: Wallace Falls and Wallace Lake Loop
searchResults.description: Begin by passing Lower, Middle, and Upper Wallace Falls before following the two-track path through the forest toward Wallace Lake. On the return trip, you will hike along the North Fork of the Wallace River to the point where it meets the main Wallace River. An early start is recommended on the weekends to secure a parking spot.

searchResults.area_name: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area
searchResults.name: West Tiger # 3 via Cable Line Trail Loop
searchResults.location_label: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description:
This trail is an alternative trail to the summit of West Tiger Summit #3. This trail follows the buried power lines straight up to the summit. There are many additional side trails if you wish to explore further.

The West Tiger Cable line is the steep way to the summit of West Tiger Mountain #3, climbing 2,000 feet to the top.

searchResults.area_name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Dirty Harry's Peak via Birdhouse Trail
searchResults.location_label: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: Harry's Peak can be accessed via Birdhouse trail. The old trailhead to Harry's Peak is now completely overgrown and no longer open. Some overgrowth will also be experienced on the trek between Dirty Harry's Balcony to Dirty Harry's Peak. Please use Birdhouse Trail on ascent and descent to avoid unsafe conditions.

searchResults.name: Seward Park Perimeter Loop
searchResults.description:
Within the Seattle city limits, Seward Park boasts 300 acres of beautiful forest land, home to eagles' nests, old-growth forest, a short bike and walking path, an amphitheater, a native plant garden, an art studio, miles of hiking trails, shoreline, beaches and more. 

Accessibility: There are 2 designated accessible spaces in the paved parking lot off Seward Park Road at the south end of the trail. Both of them are van-accessible with striped access aisles. The trail surface is paved asphalt...

searchResults.name: Mima Falls Loop
searchResults.description: This trail takes you to Mima Falls. Rather than continuing back the way you came, it follows a series of alternate trails to complete a loop. The trail is mostly shaded as it takes you through a dense forest. The trails are well-maintained, with some rocky and rooty sections. Mima Falls takes its name from the nearby Mima Mounds. Mima is a Native term meaning "a little further along." The trails are not well-marked, so downloading offline maps is recommended.

searchResults.name: Coyote Loop
searchResults.description: Forest preserve between Bellevue and Kirkland. Beautiful shady trail through a forest. Great for trail runners and equestrians. Mountain biking within the park is strictly prohibited for safety reasons. The trails are well-maintained. Bears are commonly spotted in the area. Bug spray is recommended in the spring and early summer.

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Teneriffe Falls Loop via the Mount Teneriffe Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: On the way up, you will hike through the forest filled with moss-covered trees and cross several small streams cascading down the mountain. As you make your way up the rocky switchbacks leading to the falls, you'll come to a nice viewpoint. On the descent, you will cross a scree field that offers more views before entering back into the woods.

searchResults.name: Gold Creek Pond Loop
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
During the summer, visitors can park very close to the pond. This pond may be filled in as part of a restoration project to restore the Bull Trout to Gold Creek.

The U.S. Forest Service maintains this trail.

Accessibility: 

Equipment
According to the park website, this trail is accessible for visitors using wheelchairs, mobility equipment, or strollers. All-terrain tires or adaptive equipment may be needed for the surface type and grade.

Parking 
There are 2 designated accessible spaces...

searchResults.name: Upper Thetis Lake Trail
searchResults.location_label: Thetis Lake Regional Park, British Columbia
searchResults.description:
Upper Thetis Lake is a beautiful lake surrounded by cliffs of varied heights, creating a stunning backdrop. During the warmer months, people often kayak, paddleboard, and enjoy the soothing waters. The lake's pristine surface attractively reflects the surrounding trees.

The trail consists of gravel and packed dirt. All of the sections have informative signage to guide you. You'll see a variety of ecosystems while strolling along the Upper Thetis Trail, including lakes, woodlands, and swamps....

searchResults.name: Sol Duc Falls Trail
searchResults.description: The parking lot for the trailhead is at the very end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road. This is a nice gentle and short hike through old-growth forest to a beautiful three-prong waterfall that comes from the Sol Duc River and captures rainbows in the spray.  You will pass over a few spring-fed and snow runoff creeks along the way.  Sol Duc Falls rages under a wooden bridge and the hike has a wooden platform at the end of the trail - a nice place to sit and enjoy the view!

searchResults.name: Sugarloaf Mountain and Mount Erie Loop Trail
searchResults.description: The trail begins by heading uphill through the forest towards Sugarloaf Mountain. The top of the mountain has views of the ocean and islands dotting the coastline. After this continue over to Mount Erie where you're once again rewarded with a great viewpoint. After this the remainder of the loop is mostly downhill.

searchResults.name: Pinnacle Peak Park via Cal Magnusson Trail
searchResults.description: This is a steep loop through Pinnacle Peak Park with 1000+ft elevation gain in the first mile. At the top of the climb, you will arrive at the fire tower. It is mostly wooded, but there are a few nice viewpoints along the way. There are little to no markings and may be muddy. Downloading the map ahead of time is recommended.

searchResults.name: Spruce Nature Trail and Hall of Mosses Loop
searchResults.description: This is an amazing trail through spectacular spruce forests. It takes you to the Hall of Moses and the Ho River Viewpoint under the lush rainforest. The trail begins at the parking lot next to the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center. There is also a large campground and amphitheater at the start of the trail. Keep an eye out for the flora and fauna here; the temperate rainforest is a great environment for huge trees such as Western Hemlock and Sitka Spruce to thrive.  In the creek, there may be...

searchResults.name: Rampart Ridge Loop
searchResults.description:
This moderate loop passes through forests with glimpses of the surrounding mountain vistas. Also known as "The Ramparts," this ridge is the remnant of an ancient lava flow which originated at the summit of Mount Rainier.

The trail begins at the west end of the Trail of the Shadows, approximately 0.2 miles from the trailhead if heading clockwise. The loop can be hiked in either direction, but going clockwise keeps Mount Rainier in front more of the time and is thus recommended. Walk up...

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Talus Loop Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: This loop begins by following the Mount Si Trail, and then deviates onto the Talus Loop Trail at the first major junction. There are signs in place pointing you towards the Talus Trail. The trail travels through the woods and across talus fields before arriving back at the Mount Si Trail. Follow this downhill back to the start.

searchResults.name: Weowna Park Loop Trail
searchResults.description: Weowna Park sits on a hillside above Lake Sammamish. The trails explore the dense forest and creeks that flow towards the lake. The trails are all well-defined and easy to follow. Parking is limited at the lot along W Lake Sammamish Parkway SE, so an early start is recommended especially on the weekends.

searchResults.name: Mineral Creek Falls via Hoh River Trail
searchResults.description:
For a peaceful out-and-back day hike, the first section of the Hoh River Trail is mostly level and often much quieter than other, more bustling areas of the park. The only sounds are bird songs and rushing water. Look for the beautiful cascade of Mineral Creek Falls near the turnaround spot.

As a backpacking route, this trail takes you deep into one of the world’s most famous temperate rainforests. To stay overnight, you must reserve a wilderness permit in advance through the National Park...

searchResults.name: Loop Trail via West Emerson Street Entrance
searchResults.description: The Loop Trail via West Emerson Street Entrance in Discovery Park offers a scenic hike in Seattle’s largest urban park. This trail takes you along the coastal bluffs of Puget Sound, with stunning views of the mountains and ocean. The path is well-marked, and along the route, there are interpretive signs that provide information about the park’s natural and cultural history.

searchResults.name: Ellis Cove Trail
searchResults.description: Great little hike! Some hills and stairs for a small workout, and lots of shade to keep you cool. The trail wraps around Ellis Cove and you can even see the Olympic Mountains on a clear day. The trail is well-maintained and easy to follow but is known to be muddy during the winter and spring months.

searchResults.name: Indian, Shy Bear and Quarry Loop
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description:
Highlights of this loop included waterfalls and a dense forest filled with moss-covered trees.

Please do not park on the 171st Ave SE cul-de-sac. The beginning of this trail has been rerouted to the Licorice Fern trailhead, where you can find parking at the shoulder parking on Licorice Way near the retention pond to begin the hike.

searchResults.name: Lake Angeles Trail
searchResults.description: Lake Angeles is a stunning alpine lake in the Olympic Mountains surrounded by lush montane and subalpine forests. The trail begins at the Heart O' the Hills Trailhead, next to Lake Dawn. It takes you to Lake Angeles Campground and Lake Angeles. The terrain on the path features a steady incline with some steeper sections towards the lake. The trail is well maintained, with good shade and amazing views.

searchResults.name: Staircase Rapids Loop
searchResults.description:
Staircase Rapids is a beautiful loop trail following the North Fork of the Skokomish River. The rapids is a series of faster moving water over rocks and around bends that is very scenic. 

Visitors here will also enjoy the Olympic old-growth forest with a lush understory of mosses and ferns. 

The western side of the loop typically offers more views of the river. Swimming holes in the cold river can be found throughout the hike. 

Parking is near the Staircase Ranger Station and Campground.

searchResults.name: Lake Washington North, Beach and Seminary Trail Loop
searchResults.description: Come explore the unique nature of Saint Edward State Park! This loop is a fantastic trip through a rich, native forest that is a vital home for local wildlife. As you walk, you'll see ferns covering the ground and huge Bigleaf Maple trees reaching for the sky. Look closely at the forest floor: if it’s damp, you might spot a shiny, yellow Pacific banana slug! The trail leads you to Lake Washington's undeveloped shoreline, which is a crucial spot for tiny, young salmon. Local conservation...

searchResults.name: Millersylvania Northwest Loop
searchResults.description: Discover Pass required. Cash and card payment options for single-day use. Visitors have reported the trails can be hard to follow so you may want to download the offline map before you go.

searchResults.name: Debbie's View via May Valley Loop and West Peak Trail
searchResults.description: This route starts from the state park's parking lot, passes the May Valley Loop, Bullitt Gorge, West Peak, Premier Loop trails, and the must-go Debbie's View, which is the only awesome lookout of the whole Squak Mountain.

searchResults.name: Stan's Overlook
searchResults.description: Stan's Overlook is the first stop on the Rattlesnake Mountain Trail.  A gentle hike with a nicely maintained trail. Start at Snoqualmie Point Park to access the trail. The trail is mostly wooded until you reach the overlook. At this point, there is a bench to sit at and enjoy the view of the horizon line.

searchResults.name: Madison Falls Trail
searchResults.description:
This short paved trail leads to the falls. The open field nearby is the site of the late 19th-century Sweet Family Homestead and is now used in summer for the park's horses and mules to pasture. The mules help keep backcountry trails in shape by carrying supplies for the trail crew into the wilderness, where motorized vehicles are not permitted.

Accessibility: Visitors using wheelchairs, mobility equipment, or strollers may need assistance along this entire route due to the consistent...

searchResults.name: Franklin Falls
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Striped Peak Loop
searchResults.description: Gorgeous old-growth forest trail with glimpses of the water. The elevation is a bit of a roller coaster, and the trail does get slippery when it’s raining. Trekking poles and sturdy footwear are recommended. This is a very quiet and beautiful trail. Bug spray is recommended during the summer months.

searchResults.area_name: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Talus Rocks Loop
searchResults.location_label: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: This is a wooded loop leading to Talus Rocks. This is an area where the trail travels through a narrow rocky corridor. Small woodland mammals and deer are sometimes spotted along the trail. The Tiger Mountain Trailhead is popular, so an early start is recommended on the weekends. Be cautious as poison ivy is sometimes along the trail.

searchResults.name: Index Town Wall Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
This trail doubles as the approach trail that rock climbers use to access the Index Town Walls and an awesome hike to views of Index and the surrounding area. 

Once you're at the parking lot, cross the railroad tracks and turn right to walk down the gravel path about less than half a mile to look for a red sign that says "authorized vehicles only."  Your trail begins here. Follow the blue, pink, and orange markers to follow the trail. The trail will narrow and become steeper once you're...

searchResults.name: Coal Creek Falls
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington

searchResults.name: Cheshiahud Lake Union Loop
searchResults.description:
This is a well-maintained urban paved multi-use trail with great views of the lake. It's easy to get off route at Fremont Canal. Be on the lookout for the sign for University Bridge. Some of the trail shares the road with vehicles, so using reflective materials, lights, or flagging is recommended for safety. 

Accessibility: There are at least 2 designated accessible spaces in the paved parking lot off of Westlake Avenue North at the southwest end of the trail. Both of them are van-accessible...

searchResults.name: The Washington Park Arboretum
searchResults.description:
The Washington Park Arboretum is a 230-acre hidden gem on the shores of Lake Washington. Jointly managed by the University of Washington and the city of Seattle, the arboretum harbors a dynamic assortment of plants found nowhere else. The entire park (except for the Japanese Garden) is free and open to the public year-round.

When the Graham Visitors Center parking lot is full or partially closed, there is additional parking at other access points; it is relatively easy to park elsewhere....

searchResults.name: Franklin Ghost Town Trail
searchResults.location_label: Green River Gorge Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: Follow a gentle old railroad grade into the coal-mining ghost town of Franklin, along the Green River near Black Diamond. It’s an easy walk up to the coal cart and sealed mine shaft. Follow the narrow footpath beyond to discover the powerhouse foundation and cemetery. There is a free easement through the private land to the state land. This trail and old town site is on WA state land. It is free to enter and explore. The private land owner charges a fee to park, but you can park on the side...

searchResults.name: Discovery Park Extended Loop
searchResults.description:
Starting from the trailhead, you'll descend a few steps before a gentle uphill hike. After a short, steep climb, the trail levels out. You'll cross a paved road and continue climbing. Listen to the tapping sounds of woodpeckers sometimes seen in the park.

In late winter, you might spot the white blossoms of Indian plum along the trail. In spring, look for Oregon grape's bright yellow flowers and wild currant's red blooms. The trail soon reaches the highest point on the Loop Trail, where a...

searchResults.name: Quinault Loop
searchResults.description:
The Quinault Loop Trail, also known as the Rain Forest Nature Trail, is a great way to experience the Olympic temperate rain forest and Quinault Lake. The trail has no real beginning or ending point, so you can start and stop wherever you like.    

The trail is mostly flat, with some gentle hills.  The trail follows the south shore of Quinault Lake and winds through the temperate rain forest. The forest is dense and old-growth, with lush understory of rain forest vegetation.  You'll see a...

searchResults.name: Lighthouse Point via Bowman Bay/Rosario Beach Trail
searchResults.description:
Mostly paved trail along the water, then up through the trees and back. The trail through the trees is in good condition. Not particularly steep, or strenuous. Best views are along the water. Keep an eye out for wildlife including seals and a variety of birds.

Use caution if hiking the northernmost part of this trail. It is not maintained by the parks department and is not marked. The southern section is maintained, however.

searchResults.name: Duckabush River Trail to Five Mile Camp
searchResults.description:
This trail follows the Duckabush River into The Brothers Wilderness and enters Olympic National Park around 6.7 miles.

The trail enters a burned area at around the two-mile mark and continues beyond Five-Mile Camp, the origin of the 2011 fire. Use caution when traveling and camping within the burned area, as there are many dead-standing trees and unstable surfaces as a result of the fire.

The trail is an easy grade for 2.4 miles and becomes more difficult while climbing over Big Hump. The...

searchResults.name: Hex Mountain Trail
searchResults.description:
Starts on a wide gravel/dirt path. Turns off onto a smaller trail after a mile or so. Weaves along a ridge with the lake to your left. Tons of wildflowers along the path. Steady incline the whole way up. There’s very little tree cover in the first 2 miles so on a sunny day it will be hot and unforgiving. Shade starts about 2/3rds of the way up when you’re on the final ridge section toward hex and the brush gets thicker.

Lovely hike if you’re looking for an easy summit with a simple trail to...

searchResults.name: South Tiger Mountain Loop
searchResults.description: The trails around Tiger Mountain are some of the most popular in the greater Seattle area. There are awesome views of Mount Rainier on a clear day. This loop explores the southern end of the forest and starts from Tiger Mountain Road Southeast. Some areas have been logged in recent years, so you will see trees in all different stages of growth.

searchResults.name: Watershed Park Trail
searchResults.description: A nice walk through moss-covered trees and peek-a-boo stream. The trail is well-marked and easy to follow. Keep an eye out for interesting fungi along the way. The trail can be muddy/slippery during the wet and rainy season, so watch your step. Sturdy footwear is recommended. This is a great trail for the entire family.

searchResults.name: May Valley Short Loop
searchResults.description:
This trail takes you along the May Valley Trail on a steady incline and is challenging yet enjoyable. The area can be overgrown and hard to navigate, so make sure you wear long pants and download the route beforehand. 

Route signage is marked as May Valley Loop. A Discover Pass is required. A day pass can be purchased at the trailhead.

searchResults.name: Coal Creek and Primrose Trail Loop from Lakemont Blvd
searchResults.description: This route travels through dense forest made up of moss-covered trees and along Coal Creek. There are small waterfalls and cascades along the creek to stop and admire along the way. Blackberries can be found growing alongside the trail during the summer months. The trail is well-maintained and easy to follow.

searchResults.name: Carkeek Park Loop via Piper’s Creek Trail
searchResults.description: With breathtaking vistas of Puget Sound, the hike starts in the forest that stretches down the shore. You may enjoy the views of the many towering trees that line the steep canyon walls as you follow the trail downstream. You will go via Piper's Orchard as you proceed. After crossing a small brook, the trail enters a meadow ideal for rest stops and picnic tables. Views into the Mohlendorph Creek and Venema Creek canyons are available from this vantage point. Downloading offline maps is...

searchResults.name: Dungeness Spit Trail
searchResults.description:
You will pass through the Recreation Area to reach the Wildlife Refuge.

Dungeness National Wildlife Refuge provides a great place to check out waterfowl and seabirds on the coast. It is one of the world's longest natural spit sands and can be a long walk.

That said, it's a great way to spend a nice day. The nice part is that you can turn back at any point, there are no monumental landmarks along the way that you'll miss if you don't make the end. 

That doesn't mean there is nothing to see,...

searchResults.area_name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Mailbox Peak
searchResults.location_label: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington

searchResults.name: Grand Prospect via Rattlesnake Mountain Trail
searchResults.description: Expect a lot more solitude on this approach and enjoy views of the Snoqualmie Valley, Mount Si, Mount Teneriffe, North Bend, and more. The views are some of the best in the Cascade foothills and the trail can be hiked year-round, though it can be snowy in winter and can be muddy/slippery in patches after a good rain.  Bring layers as the weather/temp can change quickly.

searchResults.name: Dash Point Trail
searchResults.description:
Located in Federal Way between Seattle and Tacoma in the Puget Sound, this park is a popular destination for hiking, biking, kayaking, fishing and recreational beach activities. Beach explorers can find starfish, crabs, birds and raptors. This 398-acre camping park features 3,301 feet of saltwater shoreline. The beach provides unobstructed views of the Puget Sound and opportunities for sea-life study.

This loop is a great day hike on well maintained trails. There are several trail options...

searchResults.name: Coal Creek Trail
searchResults.description:
A short hike through the woods while exploring the area's coal mining history.

This is an easy hike that will lead you through a historical coal mining region. While the towns are gone you will still be able to view some artifacts from the past. Along the way you will see a coal mine shaft and an information kiosk where you can learn more about its history. There are also a few railroad cart turntables but they are difficult to spot as their concrete foundations are all that is left and the...

searchResults.name: Four Cedars Outer Loop
searchResults.description:
The park provides two kitchen shelters with electricity, plus 11 sheltered and 20 unsheltered picnic tables. Kitchen shelters include picnic tables, water, sinks, and grills. Both kitchen shelters can accommodate up to 50 guests. Due to limited parking, only one shelter may be reserved at a time. Early reservations are recommended. Visitors are encouraged to carpool. To reserve a kitchen shelter, call the park at 360-456-6464.

A recreational license is required for fishing and shellfish...

searchResults.name: Goldstream Falls and Arbutus Loop
searchResults.description:
This trail begins from the Goldstream Campground parking lot and first visits the beautiful Goldstream Falls. Parking is free at the campground and but it can fill up by the middle of the day. 

The trails are clearly marked with lots of signage throughout. Bringing sturdy and waterproof shoes is recommended since this trail is a little rugged, with mud to go through and fallen branches to climb over. The trail briefly crosses through the campground and visits Arbutus Loop before heading back...

searchResults.name: Goose Rock Trail
searchResults.description: The first stretch of trail is close to the water with a view of Ben Ure Island. A well signed junction marks the start of the Goose Rock Summit Trail. This leads to the summit of Goose Rock which has an excellent view of the water. After enjoying the viewpoint, head back down towards the bridge and visitor center.

searchResults.name: Echo Peak Loop Trail
searchResults.description: This loop mostly brings hikers through dense forests, but there is a nice view as a reward along the way. Once you arrive at the top of Echo Peak there is a nice overlook where Mount Rainier is visible on a clear day. The trails are well maintained, but you should expect some mud if it has recently rained.

searchResults.name: Clark's Creek Trail
searchResults.description: This loop starts by passing the dog park and continues through the dense woods along a well-defined path. It passes several small ponds and creeks. There are not many signs or blazes along the way, and it crosses several other trails in the same park. To help navigate, it is recommended that you download the map ahead of time.

searchResults.name: Kendall Peak Lakes Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: The trail is wide and well-marked, making it an easy-grade snowshoe to the lakes during the winter months. At points, there are views across the valley looking out towards the surrounding mountains and the Summit at Snoqualmie Ski Resort. The first lake is pretty but filled with vegetation, the second lake is more open and a clear blue color.

searchResults.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: The trailhead is located along Middle Fork Road at the confluence of the Taylor River and the Middle Fork of the Snoqualmie River. The trail travels upstream, at points right along the river and at other points deeper into the forest. The trail ends at the junction with Dutch Miller Gap Trail near Nellie Falls.

searchResults.name: Beach House and Stump House via Sawmill and Big Maple Trail
searchResults.description:
The route on this page encompasses all of the Guillemot Cove Nature Reserve trails, including Sawmill, Big Maple, River, Plateau, Stump House, Beach House, Ridge, and Margaret's Trail.

This trail features a good mix of terrain, with an easy and pleasant forest experience. There are multiple ways to access the beach, making this a great option for all. Respect all postage signage for nearby private property.

searchResults.name: Soaring Eagle Park Trail
searchResults.description: This route is a series of well defined paths throughout Soaring Eagle Regional Park. The area is densely wooded with a variety of different trees. The trails are popular with hikers and mountain bikers, so expect to be sharing the trail with others. There are some rocky sections of trail, so good hiking footwear is needed.

searchResults.name: Ruby Beach
searchResults.description:
This hike is a quick stroll along the beach that shows off the beauty of the shoreline in Olympic National Park. There are towering seastacks, piles of driftwood logs, and an amazing array of wave-polished stones of all colors.

Beach 1 provides a quick hike out to a perfect lagoon for skipping stones. 

It is recommended to go at low tide to be able to explore more areas of the beach.

searchResults.name: Creyke Point and Beechey Head Loop
searchResults.location_label: East Sooke Regional Park, British Columbia
searchResults.description:
Please be very, very careful if you are a beginner hiker or the conditions are wet. There are lots of roots and rocks that make travel uneven but not difficult, but this changes when coastal rains occur. The return trail on the interior part of the loop from Beechey Head back to Aylard Farm Trailhead is wide, pretty, and quickgoing. It's definitely, a great trail for summer. Take a quick dip or relax on the sandy beach afterward.

This trail begins from the Aylard Farm Trailhead, which can be...

searchResults.name: Far Country Falls
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington

searchResults.name: Tin Mine and Davis Loop
searchResults.description:
The Tin Mine Trail and Davis Trail Loop in Green Mountain State Forest near Bremerton is just a short ferry ride from Seattle. It features a historic mine, streams, a pond, and small waterfalls.

The mountaintop view is stunning. However, watch for narrow, muddy sections after rain and snakes, and bring bug spray.

searchResults.name: Explorer Falls
searchResults.description: This route follows an old forest service road to a section of switchbacks that take you to the base of the falls. Parking is just off Monroe Camp Road, but there is not a designated trailhead or restroom facilities. The trail beyond the top of Explorer Falls can be difficult to find once you cross the stream above.

searchResults.name: Second Beach
searchResults.description:
The trailhead is on La Push Road on the Quileute Indian Reservation. The trail is wooded for the first 0.7 miles (1.1 km) and then descends to a beach with tidepools. Nearby, First Beach can be reached with vehicles and is great for surfing. Check current conditions using this webcam: http://forkswa.com/first-beach-webcam/

The Reservation has asked for visitors to ask before taking pictures of people or events, and to not remove sand, shells, driftwood, eagle feathers, broken pottery, etc....

searchResults.name: Tumwater Falls Trail
searchResults.description:
This is a picturesque trail featuring numerous waterfalls, flowers, a salmon hatchery, and fish ladders. You can get quite close to the water, and the vegetation is beautiful. 

The Olympia Tumwater Foundation maintains this trail.

Accessibility: 

Equipment
Visitors using wheelchairs, mobility equipment, or strollers may need all-terrain tires or adaptive/motorized equipment for the surface type and grade.

Parking
There are 2 designated van-accessible spaces with striped access aisles in...

searchResults.name: Puyallup Loop Trail
searchResults.description:
This loop includes several different trails including Clark's Creek, Dead Man's, Hummingbird Hill Trail, Brown Trail, Silver Creek Trail, and Meeker Creek Trail.

Portions of this loop include residential streets and neighborhoods with cars, before linking back up with the trail. Please stay on the public thoroughfares when surrounded by private property. There are more access points than what is shown on this page. You can access the loop at any point that it crosses a road. It can be easy...

searchResults.area_name: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Tradition Lake Loop Trail
searchResults.location_label: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: Begin by following the Swamp Trail, along the way there are signs telling the "Swamp Monster" story. Next, you will follow the Ruth Kees Big Tree Trail and pass the Big Tree. You will pass some small ponds along the wetlands trail. An old school bus is located along the appropriately named Bus Trail. The Around the Lake Trail leads back to the start.

searchResults.name: Shi Shi Beach Trail
searchResults.description: Journey to a place steeped in the history of the Makah People (who have been stewards of this coast for thousands of years). The Shi Shi Beach Trail begins with a flat, forested hike through towering Sitka spruce, but the middle is a long slog through unavoidable deep mud. The trail ends abruptly with a steep descent down a bluff (ropes are often present as handrails) onto the majestic beach. Along the shore, look for bald eagles and sea lions on the offshore stacks. For safety and navigation...

searchResults.name: Hurricane Hill via Hurricane Ridge
searchResults.description: Located at the end of Hurricane Ridge Road in the Olympic Mountains, the Hurricane Hill Trail is an incredible hike to a fantastic viewpoint. The trailhead starts 1.5 miles beyond the Hurricane Ridge Visitor's Center in Olympic National Park. This paved trail climbs to a panoramic view of the Olympic Range, Puget Sound, and Vancouver Island. As one of the most easily accessible locations in the Olympic Peninsula (under an hour from Port Angeles), this day hike is a popular option for...

searchResults.name: Zachs Lookout
searchResults.description:
When passing through private property easements and right-of-ways it is especially important to stay on the path and respect posted guidance. Local officials and private landowners work in partnership to provide public access to this area. Staying on the path while on private property ensures that agreements between local officials and the landowner are upheld and that this trail remains open to the public in the future.

You can find more information here:...

searchResults.name: Glacier Vista via Avalanche Lily, Dead Horse Creek and Skyline Trail
searchResults.description:
Glacier Vista is a viewpoint that provides incredible views of the Nisqually Glacier. Follow the Avalanche Lily Trail to the Dead Horse Creek Trail. Continue along the Skyline Trail to the Glacier Vista Trail. Descend the Skyline Trail back down to the trailhead to complete the loop.

This is a busy trailhead, so plan to arrive early, especially on summer weekends.

searchResults.name: Washington Park Arboretum Loop
searchResults.description:
This is a fantastic trail right in the city. There are so many different paths you can take with several parking lots along the trail. This trail is paved and circles the perimeter of the park with lots of beautiful flowers and amazing greenery. 

Accessibility: 

Equipment
Visitors using wheelchairs, mobility equipment, or strollers may need all-terrain tires or adaptive/motorized equipment for the surface type and grade.

Parking
It is unclear whether designated accessible parking is...

searchResults.name: Mount Wells Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Wells Regional Park, British Columbia
searchResults.description: This trail starts off on a moderate grade but gets steeper in the top half of the mountain. It becomes a bit more rocky with some steep ledges making it more technical, but there are chains in place to help with these sections. It's all well worth the summit and beautiful view of the city, ocean, and snow capped mountains in the far off distance.

searchResults.name: Juan De Fuca Marine Trail: Mystic Beach
searchResults.location_label: Juan de Fuca Provincial Park, British Columbia
searchResults.description:
The Juan de Fuca Marine Trail is a strenuous, multi-day (optional) hike in a rugged and isolated environment and park visitors should plan accordingly. Hikers should be prepared for uneven ground and slippery conditions on muddy trails, wooden surfaces, boulders, and rocky shorelines.

Trail improvements are scheduled to commence in the fall of each year on the Juan de Fuca Marine Trail, and may result in partial trail rerouting.

searchResults.name: Rattlesnake Ledges to East Peak
searchResults.description: This route takes hikers to the popular Rattlesnake Ledge, and then continues on to the summit of East Peak. There are awesome views of Rattlesnake Lake and the nearby mountains from the series of ledges. At East Peak, there is a bench in place to sit and enjoy the view from. The trail is well-maintained and easy to follow.

searchResults.name: Hugo Peak Trail
searchResults.location_label: Charles Lathrop Pack Experimental Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This hike takes you to the summit of Hugo Peak after a few miles through mostly forest. This trail is steep on the way up. You will reach a meadow area near the summit with benches to stop and rest. To get a good view and check out the summit, it is recommended to continue on to the viewpoint before turning around.

searchResults.name: Licorice Fern Trail to Far Country Falls
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description: Begin following Licorice Fern Trail to Licorice Way. Once you cross the street you will continue following Licorice Fern Trail to the Indian Trail. This will lead to Far Country Falls Viewpoint. On the return, you can take a spur trail up to the Far Country Lookout. From this point, you will be looking out over Renton.

searchResults.name: Ruston Way Trail
searchResults.description:
This is a beautiful paved trail along Commencement Bay that is popular with cyclists, walkers, runners, and children. Lots of parking lots along the route and lots of places to stop and eat along the water. Great route to get a taste of Old Tacoma.

Accessibility: There is 1 designated accessible space in the paved parking lot off of Ruston Way at the southeast end of the trail. It is van-accessible with striped access aisles. The trail surface is paved asphalt or concrete and smooth. It is...

searchResults.name: Mount Finlayson Trail
searchResults.description: This trail up to Mount Finlayson is a steady incline the whole way and more on the difficult end of the moderate. Near the top it gets a bit technical, with some minor scrambling over a rock face for which having good shoes is highly recommended. This trail can get quite busy, with the summit offering 360-degree views of the surrounding area.

searchResults.name: Robe Canyon Historic Trail
searchResults.location_label: Robe Canyon Historic Trail Park, Washington
searchResults.description:
The first mile is downhill, after this the trail πlevels out. The trail ends at a waterfall. Parking along the highway by the trailhead is plentiful.

The route outlined here where the path meets a tunnel. Past this there has been a series of landslides and the area is unsafe for hikers to travel through.

searchResults.name: Marymere Falls Trail from Lake Crescent Lodge
searchResults.description: This trip is about half a mile above the Marymere Falls Loop. It has two more views of the marymere fall and an additional water fall that you see at the end of the secret falls loop.

searchResults.name: Snoquera Falls Loop Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Begin by heading uphill along the Snoquera Falls Trail. As you approach the falls, there are some views looking back towards the mountains. The falls are best viewed in early spring. On the way down, you will reach the White River Trail, which leads back to the trailhead. Some stretches are made up of loose rock, so shoes with good traction are needed. The trail can be a bit hard to follow in some spots due to poor markings, so it's a good idea to download the route before you go to stay on...

searchResults.name: Granite Mountain
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Big Tree Ridge Trail
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description: This trail is one of Cougar Mountain's best. The trail conditions are typically good and are well-maintained. The trail is connected to the well-known "Broadway", Shangri-La Trail, and the Anti-Aircraft Peak, where there is a "Million Dollar View" looking to half of the Sammamish Lake. If the weather is fine, one may even see Mt Baker's snow-covered top.

searchResults.name: Skyline Loop
searchResults.description:
The Skyline Trail is the most popular route out of Paradise on the southern side of Mount Rainier. This loop has something for everyone: lush vegetation, glacier views, rivers, waterfalls, and incredible views of the surrounding area.

This “choose your own adventure” hike can be done in several ways. The loop can be done in either direction, but many people choose the clockwise route. If you’re not interested in doing the full loop, many hikers make it to Panorama Point before turning around...

searchResults.name: Wetland Plateau, Forest Ridge, Mainline, Red Alder, and Cascara Loop
searchResults.description: Paradise Valley Conservation area permits biking, hiking, and horseback riding on certain trails within the park. Part of this route along the Wetland Plateau and Forest Ridge Trail does not allow mountain biking. The Wetland Plateau Trail allows horseback riding, but the Forest Ridge Trail is for hiking only. For more information about the use types of each trail, please visit: https://snohomishcountywa.gov/DocumentCenter/View/9660/Park-Trail-Map?bidId=

searchResults.name: South Tiger Mountain Summit
searchResults.description:
This beautiful trail through the Tiger Mountain State Forest offers an unimpeded view of Mount Rainier. There is a good mix of mossy wooded areas and bare clearcut areas where you'll have stunning views to the west and the south. 

The trail near the top is narrow and overgrown with nettle and other thorny plants. Wearing protective clothing is a good idea. Parking at the trailhead is along the side of Tiger Mountain Road Southeast.

searchResults.name: Murhut Falls Trail
searchResults.description: The road leading to the trailhead is extremely rocky and full of potholes. The hike itself is well-maintained. It is an easy-to-moderate hike, with great views. Murhut Falls is a beautiful two-tiered waterfall. Use caution around the slick rocks if you try and swim in the pool beneath the waterfalls.

searchResults.name: Little Mountain Park Loop
searchResults.description:
Little Mountain Park, comprising 522 acres, is located south of Mount Vernon City limits. Follow the 1.5-mile paved road to the top of Little Mountain, an elevation gain of 934 feet. A covered viewpoint provides a spectacular look at the Skagit Valley, San Juan Islands, Olympic Mountains, and the tulip fields. The trail has many intersecting paths, and the signage can be confusing in some spots, so it is a good idea to download the route before you go to stay on track.

The north viewpoint...

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Mount Teneriffe via Mount Teneriffe Trailhead
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: The Kamikaze Trail is a very steep climb to the top of Teneriffe Mountain passing Teneriffe Falls along the way. From the top, there are great views of Mount Rainier on a clear day. After enjoying the view, hike across the ridgeline and then descend through the forest.
