The forest is dense and is filled with covered trees.

searchResults.name: Gold Creek Pond and Heli's Pond: Winter Route
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This lovely trail through the Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest is a great winter hike, perfect for beginners to learn snowshoeing. In winter, visitors must purchase a park pass at the trailhead. Snowshoes or microspikes for extra traction will be helpful to get around the pond. Enjoy the gorgeous mountain views along the way.

searchResults.name: Bridal Veil Falls-Mine Cascade
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Garfield Ledges
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Begin from the trailhead near the Taylor River and begin climbing uphill through the forest. At the top, there is a great view looking down the valley and into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. There are stairs in place to help ascend and descend some of the steeper sections of the trail which is well maintained and easy to follow.

searchResults.name: Lord Hill, Main Trail, and Temple Pond Loop Trail
searchResults.description: Hike a scenic loop trail in Lord Hill Regional Park, a favorite spot near Snohomish. This trail is a great way to experience the beautiful landscape of the Pacific Northwest. The trail takes you through a forest of Douglas fir and western red cedar, and you'll be treated to great views of the surrounding hills. The park has a history of logging, but it is now a protected area that offers a peaceful escape. You can expect to see a variety of native plants and might even spot some local...

searchResults.name: Illahee Preserve Loop Trail
searchResults.description: This is a fantastic, peaceful trail in Illahee Preserve. The trail is not always well-marked, so it's best to keep an eye on the map to ensure you are on the right path. The path begins from the parking lot off Almira Drive and winds along wide paths as it explores the park. This trail is the perfect way to get out in nature without leaving the city.

searchResults.name: Skyline Lake Trail
searchResults.description:
This trail heads uphill across the valley from Stevens Pass Ski Resort. The ski runs are visible as you hike up. The trail is steep and rocky, so good hiking footwear is recommended. Skyline Lake is a small pond surrounded by a stand of pine trees.

The trailhead also offers access to the Pacific Crest Trail.

searchResults.name: Banner Forest Heritage Park Loop
searchResults.description:
Banner Forest Hiking and Equestrian Park is a beautiful 635-acre public open space in the Olalla area. The forest, which includes trees, ponds, and wetlands, was acquired by Kitsap County in October 2000 after ten years of a community effort to preserve this resource in its present state for all citizens in perpetuity.  The trails are primarily used for hiking, equestrian riding, and mountain biking. Downloading offline maps is recommended.

Kitsap County maintains this trail network.

searchResults.name: Sauer's Mountain Trail
searchResults.description: This is a pleasant trail with stunning views. There are some steep portions with minimal shade toward the beginning of the hike. Be sure to sign the guest book at the top! If the small lot at the trailhead is full, please come back another time. Please respect the homeowners and do not try to park elsewhere near the trail. This trail begins on private property and leads into the National Forest, however, it is not maintained by the National Forest.

searchResults.name: Trillium Trail
searchResults.description: Take a deep breath and enjoy the lush, green beauty of the Trillium Trail in Bridle Trails State Park! This easy loop winds through a beautiful lowland forest, typical of the Puget Sound area. Look down for the lush, deep green sword ferns that carpet the forest floor and keep an eye out for the small white Western Trillium flowers that the trail is named after (WA State Parks). You'll be walking beneath huge Western Red Cedars and listening for birds like the loud Pileated Woodpecker high...

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Teneriffe Falls via Mount Si Trailhead
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: Located close to Mount Si, this trail leads to the fantastically steep and unusual Teneriffe Falls (formerly known as Kamikaze Falls). There are often other small waterfalls to be seen along the way. Make sure to get there early morning (or later afternoon) as trailhead parking generally fills up quickly in the morning. There are a few spots that it’s a bit difficult to follow the trail, but overall fairly well marked.

searchResults.name: Trillium Trail and Siler's Mill Trail
searchResults.description: This trail crosses some rolling terrain but is well-maintained and has easy footing. It is a good option for all ages. You are in the dense forest for the entire hike, making it a perfect spot on warmer summer days. The only exposed sunny area is a power line clear-cut. Mud should be expected if it has recently rained.

searchResults.name: Doughty Falls
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington

searchResults.name: Green Mountain via Davis and Gold Creek Trail
searchResults.description:
This loop through Green Mountain State Forest combines Gold Creek, Davis Trail (GM-6), and a logging road (GM-17), with a summit of Green Mountain along the way. There's a stunning view from the top.

Most of the trails are well maintained; however, there are stretches that contain a lot of gravel, which can be slippery. There are many trails in the park, so keep an eye on the map to stay on the correct route.

searchResults.name: West Tiger #1 and # 2 via High Point Trail
searchResults.description:
The West Tiger #1 and #2 hike offers a chance to visit some of the most picturesque areas via the High Point Trail. Particularly after rain, the trail may be muddy and damp.

On the High Point Trail, hikers first cross a powerline and then enter a verdant evergreen forest. The trail then meanders through patches of shaded wildflower meadows dotted with tall grasses. Hikers can stop along the road to see colorful wildflowers and berries. Bears are occasionally sighted in the region.

searchResults.name: Seahurst Park Loop Trail
searchResults.description: This loop starts and ends at a small but beautiful, well-maintained beach facility and some forest paths around a deep ravine. People who come here for the first time on a fine day will never be disappointed.

searchResults.name: Spruce Railroad Trail: Lake Crescent
searchResults.description:
Trail access is from either the East Beach Road or Camp David Junior Road, the Spruce Railroad Trail hugs the shore of Lake Crescent along an old railroad route. It is a continuation of the Olympic Discovery Trail.

This trail is now mostly flat and family-friendly. There are several tunnels to go through so bring a flashlight along for orientation and reflective clothing is also recommended for safety.

Accessibility: Designated accessible spaces are available in the parking lot off of East...

searchResults.area_name: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Talus Rocks
searchResults.location_label: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area, Washington

searchResults.name: Lower Thetis Lake Trail to Trillium Trail Loop
searchResults.location_label: Thetis Lake Regional Park, British Columbia
searchResults.description:
The stunning lake, encircled by towering cliffs, can be reached via the Lower Thetis Lake Trail and the Trillium Trail Loop. Thetis Lake's immaculate surface reflects the nearby trees, creating a serene environment where kayakers and paddleboarders frequently enjoy the quiet waters.

The trail comprises compacted dirt and gravel and has educational signs. You'll pass by Douglas-fir forests, Garry oak ecosystems, and springtime wildflowers. You will come to the Trillium Trail as you proceed....

searchResults.name: Pratt Balcony Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Heads up! This route is not well-marked, and parts of it can be hard to navigate. It is a good idea to download your offline map ahead of time.

searchResults.name: Woodland Plateau and Lloyd Trail Loop
searchResults.description: This loop takes you through Paradise Valley Conservation Area. The trail winds through the forest, offering shade, mushrooms, raspberries, wildflowers, and plentiful birdlife. The track is well-marked and well-maintained but be prepared for narrow passages and muddy areas. Parking is available at the trailhead.

searchResults.name: Olallie Lake via Pratt Lake Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
Begin from the Granite Mountain Trailhead located just off I-90. The trail climbs uphill through the woods and enters the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. You will loop around the lake before retracing the route back downhill to the start point. 

Campfires are not allowed anywhere on this trail. There are designated spots for tent camping.

searchResults.name: Des Moines Creek Trail
searchResults.description:
This is a nice paved trail along a ravine and creek.

Accessibility: There is 1 designated accessible space in the paved parking lot off of South 200th Street at the north end of the trail. It is not van-accessible with striped access aisles. The trail surface is paved asphalt and smooth. It is typically at least 8 feet wide. There is a painted dividing line along some of the trail which reduces the width.

The majority of the trail is estimated to be in the mostly gentle (5% or less) grade...

searchResults.name: Madison Creek to Glines Canyon Spillway Overlook
searchResults.description: Hike a unique trail with a fascinating history in Olympic National Park. The journey to the Glines Canyon Spillway Overlook takes you on a road that was once part of a dam system. The Glines Canyon Dam, completed in 1927, was removed in 2014 to restore the Elwha River, a major event in conservation history. As you walk, you'll be able to see the results of this massive project, with a wide valley that was once a lake, now a free-flowing river. The trail is mostly on a wide, old road and...

searchResults.area_name: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Section Line, Nook and Bus Trail
searchResults.location_label: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description:
This is a pleasant trail in West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area. It offers some lovely viewpoints as you hike through areas clear-cut for powerlines. 

At one point, you will pass the frame of an old school bus. Today, the bus is covered in moss and graffiti. On the way back to the trailhead, you will pass Round Lake, nestled in the forest. 

Many alternate trails intersect this path. It's recommended that you have the map handy to help you stay on the right path.

searchResults.name: Three Summits Loop Trail
searchResults.description: This loop takes hikers over the top of West Tiger #3, #2, and #1. Some areas have been logged offering impressive views of Mount Rainier along the way. While steep at points, the trails are well-defined and maintained routinely. Long stretches are through dense forest, so it is a great place to practice plant identification.

searchResults.name: Cowiche Canyon Trail
searchResults.description:
Less than three mile point-to-point with two major trailheads.  Several uphill scramble hikes with one leading to a winery.

Easy mostly level hike, unless alternate uphill trails taken.  Former railroad line.  Some brush crowding trail, but not too bad overall.  Eight bridges crossing a fast flowing (at the time) stream.  Mostly unshaded.  Toilets at trailhead.

searchResults.name: Cougar Mountain Indian Trail
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description:
This trail starts at the Licorice Fern trailhead, where you can find parking on the shoulder of Licorice Way near the retention pond to begin the hike.

The Indian Trail has a lot to offer on a short hike. There are several other trails that branch off from this trail which can provide numerous short hikes or for a full day of sightseeing. 

The Far County Falls are the main attraction on this trail. The size of the falls changes greatly depending on how much it has rained in the previous...

searchResults.area_name: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area
searchResults.name: West Tiger 3, Talus Rocks, Section Line and Bus Loop
searchResults.location_label: West Tiger Mountain Natural Resource Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: This trail is a lovely walk in the woods, with some interesting caves to explore along the way. The trail can get muddy in the winter or after heavy rain, so sturdy footwear is recommended. Downloading offline maps can help you navigate some sections of this trail. There are a few sides trails if you wish to explore the area further.

searchResults.name: Railroad Grade Trail
searchResults.description: This is a nice wide dirt path that weaves through the woods.

searchResults.name: Otter and Big Creek Falls Via Taylor River Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This route follows the Snoqualmie Lake Trail to Lipsy Lake and a series of small waterfalls and cascades. The trail also hikes along the Taylor River and several smaller tributary creeks that flow into it. If you love waterfalls, spring through early summer is the best time to visit. The falls can be nearly dry by late summer.

searchResults.name: Coal Creek Falls
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description: This is a lovely trail to a scenic waterfall. The trail wanders through lush forests and alongside a creek until you reach Coal Creek Falls. The trail is well-maintained and easy to follow but can be muddy in the winter and spring. The best time to do this hike is in the spring or after heavy rain when the waterfall is flowing at its peak.

searchResults.name: Skookum Flats Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This trail is mostly shady with large old-growth trees.  The view of the waterfall is obstructed by vine maples.  Hike up the east side of the Skookum creek for a partial view of the waterfall.  The west side of the creek is a difficult rock scramble, so this area should be avoided unless you have appropriate footwear and are comfortable hiking off-trail. This out and back can easily be adjusted to however many miles you wish to do.

searchResults.name: Wildside Trail to Shy Bear Trail to Cave Hole Trail
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description: Begin from the Red Town Trailhead and enter into the dense forest. As you look around you will see tall moss-covered trees and a fern-covered forest floor. Wooden bog bridges are in place to help navigate through sensitive areas and prevent damage. There are several trail junctions along the way, so downloading the map ahead of time is helpful to assist with navigating.

searchResults.name: Quinault Rain Forest Nature Trail
searchResults.description: This is a short and beautiful trail through the rain forest to the shore. There are lots of informational boards to read about the trees and forest itself.

searchResults.name: LBA Park Loop Trail
searchResults.description: Hike, run, or bike a scenic loop trail that has a view into the area's history at LBA Park. This is a good workout with rolling hills that wind through a beautiful forest. The park has a variety of connecting trails, so it can be helpful to download the route beforehand to make sure you stay on the loop.

searchResults.name: Ozette Triangle Trail
searchResults.description:
The Ozette Triangle is a great loop hike in Olympic National Park that can be done at almost any time of year. The biggest factor for completing the loop are the ocean tides. 

During tides higher than 5 feet (consult a tide table), certain headlands will be impassable on the beach. However, steep overland trails are available. These require clambering up steep ocean bluffs with the assistance of a rope that is tied off to a tree. 

The loop begins at Lake Ozette and you quickly cross an...

searchResults.name: Sequalitchew Loop
searchResults.description:
This trail offers hikers a great variety of scenery and terrain. Beginning from the DuPont Civic Center Parking lot, you'll head through a tunnel and down towards the shoreline. After soaking up the view, double back to the trail and turn off to take the switch back up to the top of the canyon.

Continue along the hard-packed dirt trail through the woods until you come to the edge of a neighborhood. The remainder of the trail is paved with no shade and winds through suburbia, leading you back...

searchResults.name: Mount Finlayson Loop
searchResults.description:
Mount Finlayson’s loop option is a real climb, and is best completed going clockwise if you are hoping to have the easiest route. Navigating the slick rock going down counter-clockwise, especially in slippery conditions, could be dangerous in places. It can be easy to get lost on the return part of the loop as it is not very well marked, but downloading the map in advance can help with this problem.

Overall, this is a very nice trail with good views of the Mount Baker and Bear Mountain area,...

searchResults.area_name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Winter Block via Birdhouse Trail
searchResults.location_label: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description:
The Birdhouse Trail begins with a bridge crossing and proceeds into a forested area. As signs along the trail indicate, be alert for potential cliff risks. Throughout the journey, bears in their native habitat may be seen. Sturdy footwear is required because the terrain consists of stretches of mud and rocky spots, especially in the winter when the trail can get exceptionally wet and muddy.

The trail crosses a small drainage as you go along and then starts a series of switchbacks up the...

searchResults.name: East Sooke Coast, Creyke Point and Interior Trail Loop
searchResults.location_label: East Sooke Regional Park, British Columbia
searchResults.description:
This trail begins from the Aylard Farm Trailhead, which can be accessed by following Becher Bay Road just off of East Sooke Road. It's a trail with nice ocean views throughout and fresh ocean breeze with access to a sandy beach. 

Visit the multiple viewpoints on this trail such as Beechey Head, Creyke Point, Squeaky Point, and Alldridge Point. Historic petroglyphs can be viewed at Alldridge Point. 

There are lots of roots and rocks that make travel uneven but not difficult. Definitely a...

searchResults.name: Grand Forest Park Trail
searchResults.description: Grand Forest is dominated by towering cedar, fir, and some maple trees. The area is a second-growth forest and was protected with the help of Bainbridge Island Land Trust. At one point the route will loop through an open meadow, horses are sometimes spotted grazing here. This is a great day hike that is only a short boat ride from Seattle.

searchResults.name: Squak Mountain Fireplace Trail
searchResults.description: Hikers will follow the Bullitt Fireplace Trail to the top of Squak Mountain. The summit is marked by radio towers and a few small buildings. You will pass the Bullitt Fireplace along the way. There are picnic tables near the fireplace to stop and relax at. The fireplace is all that remains of a cabin built by the Bullitt Family in 1952. The family owned much of the land in the area and later donated it to create Squak Mountain State Park.

searchResults.name: Bellevue Botanical Park and Wilburton Hill Park
searchResults.description:
This is a peaceful and beautiful loop through the botanical area and Wilburton Hill Park. As the name suggests, there are some moderately steep to steep grades. Most of the trail is a wide gravel path, but there are also narrower and uneven mulched areas.

The City of Bellevue Department of Parks and Community Services and the Bellevue Botanical Garden Society maintain this trail network.

Accessibility: 

Equipment
Visitors using wheelchairs, mobility equipment, or strollers may need...

searchResults.name: Feature Show Falls
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Heart O' the Forest Trail
searchResults.description: This out and back route is a lovely, level trek through the lush forest. It starts at Loop E in the Heart O' the Hills campground. Plenty of wildflowers, mushrooms, and wildlife along the way!

searchResults.name: Anderson Landing Trail
searchResults.description:
This scenic trail explores Anderson Landing Preserve. It begins from Warren Road Northwest and meanders along a forested trail. The route stops at several outlooks with beautiful views across the water. The surrounding forest is lush with old growth and abundant animal activity. 

The elevation gain dips and rises without too many long or steep inclines. Some sections can get narrow due to encroaching vegetation. The path is often muddy and slippery, especially near the streams.

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Mount Si Loop
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description:
This loop combines the official new Mount Si Trail with the Old Mount Si Trail, which is now rarely used by hikers, with the Douglas Fir Trail (also rarely used but in perfect condition) as the connector to the Boulder Garden Loop Trail. It starts and ends at the Little Si Trailhead, so it merges with the Little Si Trail at the lower part. The route stops short of the actual summit, so if you want to reach the top, you will have to tackle a challenging incline with a scramble. 

The trail is...

searchResults.name: Maple Valley and Steam Donkey Loop
searchResults.description: Begin by following the Maple Valley Trail. You will cross over Phantom Creek and travel through dense forest. The Steam Donkey trail crosses Phantom Creek again along with some other small streams. This will lead back towards the Ranger Station and your start point. The trail is well-marked and easy to follow.

searchResults.name: Birds Nest and Lookout Beach
searchResults.description:
This is a fantastic trail with amazing mountain views, a beautiful beach, and stunning water views along the trail. There are incredible vistas throughout the park and from the lookouts, including Mount Rainier and sunset views. There are wooden lookout decks, and you can see the Olympic mountain range on clear days. 

The trail passes through meadows, forests, and along the beach. Be aware of steep stairs at the water's edge of the trail. You may also encounter wildlife. There is plenty of...

searchResults.name: Little Mashel Middle Falls
searchResults.location_label: Charles Lathrop Pack Experimental Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Fred's Railroad and Wilderness Peak Loop
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description:
This beautiful and varied trail is perfect for hiking and running, though it can sometimes be steep. Starting from the Sky Country Trailhead, the route includes the Oldman's Trail, Fred's Railroad Trail, and Wilderness Peak.

 Most of the trails are shaded, and there are no real viewpoints. The path offers a mix of wide dirt paths, single track, and metal grate duckboards. However, be cautious, as sections of the trail can become muddy after rain, potentially causing puddles and wet...

searchResults.name: Lake Washington North Trail to South Canyon Trail to Orchard Loop
searchResults.description: Step into history at Saint Edward State Park as you explore a beautiful forest that was once the grounds of the Saint Edward Seminary. Your journey follows the North Trail downhill through a lush canopy of tall Douglas-fir and Western Redcedar trees. You will head toward the shoreline of Lake Washington, the largest undeveloped stretch of lakefront in the area! Along the way, keep an eye out for the vibrant green moss covering the huge Bigleaf Maples. After enjoying the beach, the South...

searchResults.name: Rosario Head Trail
searchResults.description: This is a lovely hike with beautiful ocean views. There are also tide pools to explore along the way. Even though this is a short hike, you can spend hours here taking in the scenery and exploring the beaches. There are many beautiful wildflowers in the late spring and early summer. The weather is often windy and overcast, so bring plenty of layers.

searchResults.name: Trillium Trail and Pipeline Regional Trail
searchResults.description:
The Trillium Trail and Pipeline Regional Trail pass through a picturesque woodland landscape with ponds and wetlands. The trails meander through a second-growth forest abundant in maples, cottonwoods, Douglas firs, and cedars. 

The trails have gentle terrain and are primarily dirt trails, with some sections covered in gravel. As you hike, the trails weave in and out of gullies. There are some uneven and rocky sections with exposed roots to navigate.

searchResults.name: Old Pipeline Bed Trail
searchResults.description: Hikers will begin by crossing the Wenatchee River via an old bridge spanning the river. A wide, well-defined path follows the river on the opposite bank. At points, there are some good spots to access the water and cool off. Eventually, the trail peters out where the banks leading into the river get too steep and loose.

searchResults.name: Franklin Falls via National Forest Development Road 58
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: To access Forest Rd 58 you can park south of I-90 at the base of the Summit of Snoqualmie and walk up the interstate, or park at the PCT parking area on the north side of the highway. You will then walk along the road to access the trail that leads down to the Snoqualmie River and the waterfall. During the winter microspikes are recommended since the trail is often very icy.

searchResults.name: McLane Creek Woods Trail
searchResults.description: This is a well-maintained trail with signage throughout. The trail takes you to a beaver pond where there are benches for you to sit and watch the ducks and other birds. The second part of the trail takes you through a forest. The trail is relatively flat and is great for the entire family. Parts of this trail is ADA accessible.

searchResults.name: Pyramid Mountain Trail
searchResults.description:
Parts of this trail cross unstable, steep terrain in which many experienced hikers have encountered dangerous situations. Please use extreme caution when crossing slide areas.

The Pyramid Peak Trail can be accessed from Camp David Junior Road on the North shore of Lake Crescent. The trail and climbs about 2,600 feet in 3.5 miles (792 meters in 5.6 km), so bring your hiking poles and be prepared to climb! Like Mount Storm King, the summit has a fantastic panoramic view of the lake and Strait...

searchResults.name: Blackbird Island Trail
searchResults.description:
Walk around an island in beautiful Waterfront Park in Leavenworth. Enjoy the sounds of birds calling, fish jumping, and plenty of informative signs telling the history of the area.

You don't have to go very far from the hubbub of activity in downtown Leavenworth to find the delightful promenade for a leisurely stroll or paths on which to take a bicycle ride. You can laze the day away in serene pockets of picnicking pleasure, which are located in a totally natural environment.

If a long and...

searchResults.name: Whistle Lake Trail
searchResults.description: This is a very picturesque hike that loops around a lake with just enough elevation to get your heart pumping. There are beautiful wildflowers in the late spring and early summer. The trail can get muddy at times, so sturdy footwear is recommended. There are nice views throughout. This is a great trail for the entire family.

searchResults.name: Clear Creek Trail
searchResults.description: A well-maintained trail great for walking, jogging & biking. There is a dog park as well. Parking is available on Silverdale Way.

searchResults.name: Raven and Coyote Trail Loop
searchResults.description: Explore the gentle paths of the Coyote and Raven Trails, a wonderful loop in Bridle Trails State Park. This forested land rests on the traditional territories of the Coast Salish Indigenous people. Long ago, the old logging roads used to transport timber became the foundation for the 28 miles of walking trails that exist today. The names of the trails are inspired by the local wildlife—keep a lookout for squirrels, raccoons, or the trail’s namesake, the raven. Since some sections, especially...

searchResults.name: Point Defiance Park Inner Loop
searchResults.description: Accessibility: Some parts of this trail may be difficult for wheelchair and stroller users. This trail is partially paved (if parking by the zoo) and partially dirt. It is estimated to be mostly gentle (5% or less) with steep sections (8 -12%) at about 0.3, 1.9, and 3.4 miles when going counterclockwise. After rainstorms, the trail may be muddy and slippery and roots or rocks exposed. The most accessible part of the area which is all paved but shares the roadway with motor vehicles at time is...

searchResults.name: Kennedy Falls Trail
searchResults.description:
The 'Private Property' sign at the trailhead refers to Hunting, Fishing, and Gathering ONLY. Other non-motorized recreation is allowed.

This route follows a forest road leading to the Falls Trail. The Falls Trail travels through the woods downhill towards Kennedy Falls along Kennedy Creek. There is an upper and lower falls you can visit.

searchResults.name: Sammamish River Trail
searchResults.description:
This is a converted rail trail from Redmond to Kenmore in the eastern suburbs of Seattle and is popular with cyclists.

Accessibility: 

Equipment
Visitors using wheelchairs, mobility equipment, or strollers may need all-terrain tires or adaptive/motorized equipment for the surface type and grade.

Parking
It is unclear whether designated accessible parking is available near the trailhead.

Surface
The trail surface is paved asphalt and is typically at least 8 feet wide with a painted...

searchResults.name: Beach and Outbound Trail
searchResults.description: This beautiful walk through the tall cedar trees meanders along a little stream, crossing several bridges along the way. The trail features wooden boardwalks with grates, well-maintained wood-framed steps, ramps, and benches. Some places can become muddy and slippery after rain, so sturdy footwear is recommended. The trail begins and ends at the Thames Creek Trailhead parking lot.

searchResults.name: Vesper Peak
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Mount Rainier Overlook via River and Katie's Trail
searchResults.description:
Here you will find a beautiful web of trails and fall foliage, along with lovely views of Rainier. Parts of this trail get steep and muddy (near the river) so you'll want to bring a good pair of shoes. You may spot fishermen along the river who are looking to catch some salmon!

Due to the many intersecting trails along this loop, it's recommended that you download the route ahead of time to avoid getting lost.

searchResults.name: Bellefields and Heritage Loop Trail
searchResults.description: This route connects two interpretive loops that explore the wetlands habitat of Mercer Slough. You'll get the opportunity to check out many of the information boards and learn about the unique habitats at the park.  During the winter months, and after big rains, sections of these wetland trails can get extremely boggy - especially the trail around the Mercer Slough Blueberry Farm. If this is the case, you can alternatively continue straight on the Heritage Trail towards the Ostbo Boiler...

searchResults.area_name: Woodard Bay Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Woodard Bay Loop Trail
searchResults.location_label: Woodard Bay Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description:
There are three trail options with two different trailheads, some paved and some dirt. All are good for families and have nice views of Woodard Bay.

Accessibility: There is 1 designated accessible space in the paved parking lot off of Woodard Bay Road Northeast at the south end of the trail. It is van-accessible with striped access aisles. The trail surface is packed gravel, paved asphalt, or natural dirt surface and typically at least 3 feet wide. The most accessible portion of the trail is...

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Mount Teneriffe via Kamikaze Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: The ascent of Mount Teneriffe via the Kamikaze Trail is a thrilling and rigorous ridge-summit adventure in the Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area near North Bend, Washington. You’ll begin on forested logging-road grade toward Teneriffe Falls, then shift into the “Kamikaze” section—an unrelenting climb, often steep and exposed, straight up toward the ridge crest. Higher up, you’ll traverse a ridge with sparse vegetation, loose rock, and dramatic exposure before reaching the summit at...

searchResults.area_name: Sooke Hills Wilderness Regional Park Reserve
searchResults.name: Mount Braden Loop
searchResults.location_label: Sooke Hills Wilderness Regional Park Reserve, British Columbia
searchResults.description:
The first three kilometres are very gentle, the path before the summit loop is flat and gravel. 

Once you reach the incline on Braden Summit Trail the path becomes less maintained and the markers can be difficult to locate. Downloading the map is recommended as cell service is unreliable in this area. There are some areas that are very steep and require scrambling, with large steps up onto and down from rocks.

searchResults.name: Mount Dickerman
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Goose Rock Summit via Cranberry Lake and North Beach Trail
searchResults.description:
This trail offers hikers many stunning views of the bridge and the bay. Begin by making your way along the coastline of Deception Pass State Park through various campsites and parking lots before making a steady incline up to Goose Rock. 

Goose Rock is a great place to take a break or have a bite to eat while enjoying the far-reaching views over the ocean. The trails are not well-marked, so stay alert and keep an eye on the map.

searchResults.name: Saltwater State Park Loop
searchResults.description: This is a popular state park in the Seattle-Tacoma region with picnic facilities along the beach and a campground in the woods. The trail is in well-maintained condition for about 1.5 miles of walk or hike in the woods.

searchResults.name: Green Mountain via Wildcat Trail
searchResults.description: The top of Green Mountain offers views of Mount Rainier and Seattle on clear days. The trail passes through the woods and along the perimeter of areas that have been logged in recent years. Some sections of the trail are very rocky and covered in shale, so good hiking shoes are necessary. Dirt bikes are permitted in some areas.

searchResults.name: Double Peak Loop
searchResults.description:
Beautiful woodland trail featuring lush forest, a viewpoint of the valley, and a stone fireplace.

Discovery Pass is required for parking but there is a neighborhood another half a mile away across the road with street parking.

searchResults.name: Capitol Lake Trail
searchResults.description:
Capitol Lake is an artificial lake surrounded by gravel and paved trails that are popular for walking, running, and cycling with people of all ages.

Accessibility: There are 2 designated accessible spaces in the paved parking lot off of Deschutes Parkway Southwest at the southwest end of the trail. Both of them are van-accessible with striped access aisles. The trail surface is paved concrete or gravel. It is typically at least 6 feet wide. 

The majority of the trail is estimated to be in...

searchResults.name: South Bluff, Ridge, Piper's Creek, North Traverse, and Grand Fire Loop
searchResults.description:
This relatively flat trail starts from Carkeek Park Beach Parking Lot and takes visitors through beautiful Carkeek Park. The route features stunning views across the water and travels alongside gorgeous, tranquil creeks. 

The path is well-shaded but intersects with many different trails, so it's best to keep an eye on the map. Plenty of amenities along the way, including restrooms, a playground, and a water refill station, are a short distance from the trailhead.

Note: The trail is...

searchResults.name: Evans Creek Preserve from Sahalee Way
searchResults.description: Start your hike from Evans Creek Preserve Upper Parking Lot. You'll follow a well-marked trail from here as it winds through picturesque woodlands. The trail crosses many babbling streams with bridges and features gorgeous meadow views.  The trail can get muddy in wet conditions, especially around the creeks. There is a restroom roughly halfway along this trail.

searchResults.name: Whale Trail from Solstice Park
searchResults.description: Lincoln Park is a multi-purpose park on a bluff above Puget Sound. The park has almost five miles of trails, picnic shelters, playfields, and the Colman Pool—a heated saltwater pool and bathhouse. This route starts at Solstice Park and crosses the road (take extra caution here) to the Whale Trail, a gorgeous sandy trail along the coastline. Enjoy the gorgeous views and take a series of trails on the east end of the park to head back.

searchResults.name: Lower Big Quilcene to Notch Pass Trail Junction
searchResults.description: This trail is a peaceful and scenic hike through the woods, and is well-maintained. The trail is mostly shaded with soft elevation decline to a beautiful bark shanty at the bottom to cool off and have lunch. There is great river access along this trail. There can be mosquitos in the spring/early summer, so bringing bug spray is recommended.

searchResults.name: Big Gulch Trail
searchResults.description: Hike a scenic trail that is a hidden gem in Mukilteo. The Big Gulch trail takes you on a peaceful journey through a ravine, where you can escape the city and enjoy the sounds of nature. The area has a history of logging in the early 1900s, and remnants of old logging roads can still be seen. As you walk, you'll be surrounded by towering trees like Douglas fir and western red cedar. The trail can be a bit muddy in spots, so be sure to wear sturdy shoes.

searchResults.name: Mount Rose Trail
searchResults.description: This is a steep and challenging climb to the top of Mount Rose. Sturdy footwear and trekking poles are recommended for the steep and rocky terrain. The views from the top are well worth the effort. You will have panoramic views of Lake Cushman and the surrounding mountains. Hike this trail on a clear day for the best views.

searchResults.name: Twanoh Trail
searchResults.description:
This loop trail takes you through Twanoh State Park, winding through lush forests and alongside a creek. Be prepared for steep sections with rocks and roots—sturdy footwear is recommended, as some parts can be slippery. In the spring, you'll find beautiful wildflowers. Don’t forget to bring bug spray to protect against mosquitoes.

The trailhead is accessible from State Route 106, where parking, restrooms, a picnic area, and a campground are available.

searchResults.name: Dash Point State Park Loop via Beach Trail
searchResults.description: There is an excellent network of trails exploring the Dash Point State Park, and this route takes in many of the highlights. The trail is well-maintained and mostly follows multiple creeks. You'll pass bridges, stairs, ferns, streams, wild ginger and other native plants, and lots of birdlife. The path is almost entirely shaded by the beautiful forest. Some of the trails are not well-marked, so downloading offline maps can be helpful.

searchResults.name: Coal Creek to Primrose Trail
searchResults.description:
The Primrose Trail will take you along a creek with a few small waterfalls and several crossings over wooden bridges. Along the way, you'll pass by Sand Stone Falls, one of Coal Creek's tributaries.

The trail is well-maintained and mostly shaded by trees, but be ready for some narrow sections with roots, rocks, and mud. Along the way, look for various types of berries.

Named after a coal seam mined in the 1800s, the Primrose Trail has almost all traces of mining activities covered by...

searchResults.name: North Beach and Hidden Valley Loop
searchResults.description:
This is a gorgeous trail that explores Discovery Park's northwestern shoreline. Along the way, you will see stunning views of the beach, ocean, and greenery.

There are lots of stairs along the way, some of which are broken, and there isn't always a railing, so watch your step. Some sections of the path through the forest can get quite muddy after rain, so proper footwear is recommended. Many trails weave throughout the park, allowing you to easily adjust the length of your adventure. 

Dogs...

searchResults.name: Iron Horse Trail: Homestead Valley Trailhead to Mine Creek
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: The Iron Horse Trail is a well-maintained, crushed gravel path traveling along the hillside above the Snoqualmie River. The trail takes you over train trestles and has great views along the way. It is a perfect outing for families to explore via foot or bike. The route outlined here returns after crossing the Mine Creek Trestle.

searchResults.name: Japanese Gulch Loop Trail
searchResults.description: Good local trail to hike, walk, run, or ride. Some nice views and a fairly well-maintained trail. Trails exist on both sides of the train tracks that run through the center of the park. This trail crosses many other trails in the same park, so be sure to pay close attention to the way back as it can be difficult to navigate the turn-offs. Downloading offline maps is recommended.

searchResults.name: North Beach to Goose Rock
searchResults.description:
This trail takes you to Deception Pass State Park. The first part follows the North Beach Trail along the coastline with beaches before joining the Goose Rock Perimeter Trail, which climbs steeply to the summit of Goose Rock.

The trailhead includes large parking, restrooms, and the Cranberry Lake Campground.

searchResults.name: Holder Ridge Trail
searchResults.description: Trail begins across the forest road from the parking lot. Easy hike shared with horses and bikes with a few views along the way. Fairly well maintained but some muddy spots.

searchResults.name: Central Peak, West Peak, and Debbie's View Loop
searchResults.description:
It is a beautiful hike with a challenging climb to the destination. Looking out from Debbie's View makes the whole hike worthwhile, with expansive panoramic views from the Cascades to Tacoma!

Make sure to have this trail map downloaded, as the area has many intersecting trails.

searchResults.name: Whitaker Peak and Shy Bear Loop Trail to Doughty Falls
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description:
This trail begins with a steep climb to Whitaker Wilderness Peak, the highest point in Cougar Mountain Park. Although the summit doesn't offer views due to dense vegetation, there’s a giant wooden chair for relaxation. The trail leads through a beautiful shaded forest with ferns and large Douglas fir trees.

The trail continues to Shy Bear Pass and Doughty Falls Viewpoint. During most summer and fall days, the waterfall is barely a trickle over large moss-covered rocks. To see the falls at...

searchResults.name: Mount Manuel Quimper Extended Loop
searchResults.location_label: Sea to Sea Regional Park, British Columbia
searchResults.description:
Mount Manuel Quimper Extended Loop is a fun and challenging route with wonderful views. On a clear day, you can see all the way back to Victoria, Mitchelson, East Sooke, and the mountains to the north. There is no scrambling or intimidating drop-offs. Some of the trails are shared with mountain bikers, and therefore the trails can be dusty and steep, or wide and flat, but overall a great and scenic climb up!

There is a parking lot and public washroom facilities at the trailhead. 
Keep in...

searchResults.name: Umtanum Creek Falls Trail
searchResults.description:
The trail meanders by a stream through aspen, birch, and pine groves until it reaches a small basalt column cirque with a waterfall. Reaching the waterfall is rocky and requires some light scrambling, so make sure you have proper footwear. 

The trail is best from spring through fall, but it is often navigable with snowshoes or another traction device during the winter months. The trail is overgrown, and rattlesnakes are sometimes spotted during the summer, so keep pets on leash, wear long...

searchResults.name: North, Beach, South Canyon, Orchard, Juanita, Arrowhead Loop
searchResults.description:
Starting from the Lodge at Saint Edward State Park, this trail winds through lovely woodland and offers magnificent views of Lake Washington. Keeping on track can be tricky, so keep an eye on the map.

The forest scenery along the trail is beautiful, and there is plenty of birdlife to spot in and around the lake. Some parts of the trail can get muddy in wet conditions, so shoes with good grip are recommended.

searchResults.name: Ira Spring Memorial Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: The Ira Spring Trail climbs up through the forest to a point where there is a great view of Mount Rainier. After enjoying the view, you will head downhill towards Mason Lake. After resting at the lake you will retrace your footsteps back to the start. Some areas are very rocky, so good hiking shoes are needed.

searchResults.name: Mount Ellinor Winter Route
searchResults.description:
This is an adventurous mountaineering trail through the Olympic National Forest to the summit of Mount Ellinor. If you're here in winter, you'll need spikes and an ice axe to make it to the summit and glissade back down the chute. 

Take your time on the way down, as there are some holes to avoid in the chute. On the way up, there's a lookout point with a perfect view of Mount Rainer. You'll have an incredible view of the Olympic Range from the summit.

searchResults.name: Shoreview and Boeing Creek Loop
searchResults.description: This is a great trail with several paths and loops that run along the creek.

searchResults.name: Snow Lake Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
Starting at the Alpental Ski Area and leading up to the incredible Snow Lake, this is one of the most popular hikes in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. The route starts by climbing alongside the South Fork Snoqualmie River with Snoqualmie Mountain on your right. You’ll pass by numerous waterfalls and follow steep switchbacks on your way up to the destination.

Start your journey at the parking lot next to the Snow Lakes Trailhead, about 1.5 miles north of the freeway exit for Snoqualmie Pass. The...

searchResults.name: Sugarloaf Mountain Trail
searchResults.description: This trail is a very pleasant path through a nice lush forest. It is also a good cardio/leg workout as it’s a pretty steady incline the entire way up. But the overlook at the top is totally worth it. It can sometimes be difficult to navigate the area, so downloading offline map is highly recommended.

searchResults.name: Rabbit Trail to Echo Point to Three Lakes Trail Loop
searchResults.description: This is a wonderful trail in Spring Lake/Lake Desire Park. The trailhead is located at the end of a cul-de-sac in a residential area. There are lots of intersecting trails along the way, so you should have the map handy to make sure you remain on the right path. There is plenty of shade along this walk and a nice mix of terrain to traverse. If you're visiting in the warmer months, bring bug spray.

searchResults.name: West Tiger #3, #2, #1 via Cable Line
searchResults.description: This hike starts off via the cable line route to West Tiger #3. Most of the elevation gain happens in this section. Just before you reach #3 enjoy the view to the East towards Mt. Si. There is another smaller view point midway of #3 and #2 towards West looking at the southern tip of Lake Washington. The best views are at #1 where you can see the Olympic range and Mt.Rainier. The way down is long and gradual with plenty of opportunities to trail run.

searchResults.name: Matheson Lake Trail
searchResults.location_label: Matheson Lake Regional Park, British Columbia
searchResults.description: This is a great trail that will showcase some great British Columbian lakes with nice views of the lake and small islands. Overall, it is great for the whole family, but is definitely on the more moderate end of easy. This stunning trail follows the lake through really splendid forests, sometimes at a distance from the lake, so you will have a nice variety of lakeside hiking and forest trails. Hikers will really enjoy this and the creekside trail to Roche Cove where you can join the Galloping...

searchResults.area_name: Tradition Plateau Natural Resource Conversation Area
searchResults.name: Swamp, Ruths Kees Big Tree, and Bus Trail Loop
searchResults.location_label: Tradition Plateau Natural Resource Conversation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: Along the Swamp Trail, there are signs along the trail telling the story of the "Swamp Monster". On the Big Tree Trail, there is a sign pointing out the namesake Big Tree. You will pass some small ponds before arriving at the old bus. The bus is in very rough condition and only the frame remains. The start point is at the Tiger Mountain Trailhead.

searchResults.name: Granite Mountain Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Granite Mountain Trail in Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest follows a steep route up with some light scrambling to the beautiful summit of Granite Mountain, where hikers will find a lookout cabin/fire tower. Visitors will be treated to spectacular views of the surrounding alpine lakes and peaks, including Mount Rainier on a clear day to the south. This trail travels through potential avalanche terrain, so research conditions before heading out during winter months. A Federal Northwest...

searchResults.name: Bothell Landing Trail
searchResults.description:
This is a pleasant paved multi-use trail alongside a river. For a longer route, consider connecting to the Burke-Gilman Trail.

Accessibility: There are 2 designated accessible spaces in the paved parking lot off of Northeast 180th Street at the northeast end of the trail. Both of them are van-accessible with striped access aisles. The trail surface is paved asphalt and smooth. It is typically at least 8 feet wide. There is a painted dividing line along some of the trail which reduces the...

searchResults.area_name: Padilla Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve
searchResults.name: Padilla Bay Trail
searchResults.location_label: Padilla Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve, Washington
searchResults.description:
Padilla Bay is a shallow tidal bay. This trail is gravel and heads along the bay shore.

Accessibility: 

Equipment
Visitors using wheelchairs, mobility equipment, or strollers may need all-terrain tires or adaptive/motorized equipment for the surface type and grade.

Parking
There are 2 designated accessible parking spaces in the paved parking lot off State Route 20. 

Surface
The trail surface is packed gravel and is typically at least 5 feet wide.

Grade

searchResults.name: Fort Ebey Bluff Trail
searchResults.description: This trail begins at the parking lot off Fort Ebey State Park Road, where restrooms, a picnic area, and the Cascadia Marine Trail Campsite are available. It takes you to Ebey's Landing National Historical Reserve. It’s a beautiful coastal hike along the bluffs with stunning ocean views, a historic military bunker, and Fort Ebey.

searchResults.name: High Hut Snowshoe Trail
searchResults.description:
Hike or snowshoe a rewarding trail to a high hut with incredible views of Mount Rainier. The High Hut trail is a local favorite for a winter adventure and a great way to escape the crowds. The trail is on a wide, unmaintained road that takes you through a beautiful forest of Douglas fir and western hemlock. The hut at the top is a great place to warm up and enjoy the views of the surrounding mountains. The trail is a good workout and can be a bit steep in spots.

Driving to the trail head,...

searchResults.area_name: Sooke Hills Wilderness Regional Park Reserve
searchResults.name: Sugarloaf and Townsend Hill Loop
searchResults.location_label: Sooke Hills Wilderness Regional Park Reserve, British Columbia
searchResults.description: Sugarloaf and Townsend Hill Loop is a challenging but rewarding hike with great signage and fantastic views. The parking lot at the trailhead has ample space. There are washroom facilities before you head on your way. The main trail is a steady ascent with some steep sections. There is also some light scrambling if you choose to summit. Enjoy the woods and keep an eye out for wildlife.

searchResults.name: Olallie Lake
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Coal Creek Falls via Nike Horse Trail
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description: The start of this trail can be hard to find. Make sure you are following the Horse Trail versus the Old Man Trail. Nike Horse will lead to Cave Hole Trail. Follow Cave Hole briefly before turning onto Coal Creek Falls Trail. Coal Creek is a small but pretty waterfall. It is best visited during the spring, it can be dry in the summer months.

searchResults.name: Snow Lake Trail to Source Lake Spur Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This popular trek leads into the heart of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, offering a classic Pacific Northwest experience. You will begin at the Alpental parking lot and climb through a lush forest before the landscape transforms into rugged talus slopes. The spur to Source Lake provides a quiet detour to the headwaters of the Snoqualmie River, though the path across the boulder field requires careful footing. Once you reach the saddle, you are rewarded with a sweeping view of Snow Lake, a...

searchResults.name: Alki Trail to Hamilton Viewpoint and Seacrest Parks
searchResults.description:
This is a portion of the Alki Trail between Riverside and the Port of Seattle Jack Block Park, this trail follows the northern and eastern shore of West Seattle along Alki Avenue and has beautiful views of Puget Sound and the Olympic Mountains. Largely riding on a widened sidewalk separated from traffic by a parking lane and curb, traffic on the trail is separated for bikes and walkers, providing a less stressful experience for walkers and cyclists alike.

Accessibility: 

Equipment
This...

searchResults.name: Sky Country to Harvey Manning Loop
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description: Quite a few loops can be designed between the Sky Country Trailhead and the Harvey Manning Trailhead (formerly Anti-Aircraft Trailhead) with gentle grade. The trails are well-maintained, clearly marked, and in the shade of pleasant woodland. This is a great area for a quick hike if you are short on time or trying to get outside after work.

searchResults.name: Trillium Trail Loop
searchResults.description:
The Trillium Trail comprises gentle ascents and descents. As you hike, you will be encircled by a vivid green landscape, with pine, hemlock, and Douglas-fir trees rising above the forest floor and ferns along the trail. There is a lot of wildlife, including squirrels, deer, and birds. 

Boardwalks along this trail lead around the lake and offer great views of the surrounding forest and water. At the trail's end, a canopy of mountain hemlock, western red cedar, western hemlock, and silver fir...

searchResults.name: Wallace Lake via Woody and Greg Ball Trail
searchResults.description: Begin near the Wallace Falls State Park Campground to access the Woody Trail. The trail travels above the Wallace River, near the confluence with the north fork, you will head up to the Greg Ball Trail. This trail leads to Wallace Lake which is a very serene body of water. You will retrace the same route back to the start point.

searchResults.name: Falls View Canyon Trail
searchResults.description: This well-maintained path leads to a waterfall along the Big Quilcene River. At points, you will be inland and further from the river making your way through the forest. The start point is right near the entrance to Falls View Campground off Olympic Highway/Route 101. There is plenty of parking near the trailhead.

searchResults.name: Shangri La and Anti-Aircraft Ridge Loop Trail
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description:
Located in the "Issaquah Alps," Cougar Mountain showcases a variety of natural features from forests and waterfalls to meadows and cliffs. Sweeping vistas of the Cascades, Lake Sammamish, and Bellevue, Seattle, and beyond can be found at different points throughout the park.

There is a group of trails and loop options that begin at the Anti-Aircraft peak trailhead, including the anti-aircraft ridge.

searchResults.name: Lipsy Lake
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: McCormick Forest Park Loop
searchResults.description: This pretty trail is perfect for a quick early morning walk through McCormick Forest Park. The fire station across the road has a parking lot, or you can park along Bujacich Road at the trailhead. These well-maintained trails can be a little tricky to navigate, so keep an eye on the map to help you stay on track. The terrain is relatively flat, with a bit of an incline in the second half to get the heart pumping.

searchResults.name: Third Beach Trail to Taylor Point
searchResults.description: The trailhead is located on La Push Road, 12 miles (19 km) west of US 101. The trail descends through the forest to a scenic, sandy beach (Third Beach). There are a series of ropes and ladders to get to Taylor Point. The beach near Taylor Point is a rocky stretch of coast with sea stacks visible offshore.

searchResults.name: Main Trail and Pipeline Trail Loop
searchResults.description: Starting from the parking lot on 150th Street, this trail winds through Lord Hill Regional Park. It passes through scenic woods and by Beaver Marsh Lake. There is a good amount of shade along this trail, but it can get muddy in wet conditions. Parking can fill up quickly on weekends, so arriving early is best. A short distance south of the trailhead, additional parking is available.

searchResults.name: Spine Trail
searchResults.description:
This trail leads hikers from the parking area near the Rhododendron Garden to the Gig Harbor Viewpoint and back again. It runs in a straight line through Point Defiance Park, and the blue arrows make it easy to follow. 

It's a beautiful trail through the rainforest, with lots of pretty moss and ferns to admire. Certain sections can get muddy if it has rained in the previous few days, so come prepared. The bathrooms at the lookout are closed in winter.

searchResults.name: Squaxin Park Loop
searchResults.description:
This lovely wooded trail is located just north of downtown Olympia, near a beautiful residential neighborhood. Beginning from the Squaxin Park Trailhead, you'll take an amazing short walk amongst tall trees down to a rocky beach.

This is a peaceful and well-shaded area to come for a walk. It can be muddy at the shoreline during low tide. Some parts of the trail are not well marked or identified, so downloading the map is a good idea.

searchResults.name: Five Mile Drive
searchResults.description:
The outer loop section of Five Mile Drive is now permanently closed to vehicles. Pedestrians, runners, and cyclists are able to enjoy this forest experience free from conflict with motorized vehicles. Many dirt trails connect for users who would like a longer trip. There is a cycling lane with a painted dividing line next to the road.

For more information about the vehicle closure, visit: https://www.metroparkstacoma.org/point-defiance-outer-loop/

Visitors using...

searchResults.name: Goose Rock Perimeter Trail and Discovery Trail from Ranger Station
searchResults.description: This three mile hike around goose rock provides a variety of great scenery and topography.

searchResults.name: May's Creek Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Please be aware that Google Maps will provide incorrect directions. Turn onto 429th Street Southeast and the trailhead is at the end of the road. Along the way, you will pass a viewpoint where Mount Index and the Skykomish River valley are visible. After this, you will continue to May Creek Falls. Some areas have been logged in recent years.

searchResults.name: Anderson Cove and Copper Mine Loop
searchResults.location_label: East Sooke Regional Park, British Columbia
searchResults.description:
A great loop with amazing views of Iron Mine Bay. Park at the end of a little gravel road. The trails are pretty wide for a good chunk of the hike, but gets a bit narrow and a little overgrown when you hit Coast Trail, the views are well worth it. 

Be cautious on the Coast Trail as it can feel narrow and there is a significant drop. The hike back on Anderson Cove trail portion also has some nice vistas and elevation that gets the heart pumping a bit.

Overall, inclined and declines aren't...

searchResults.name: Beechey Head Loop
searchResults.location_label: East Sooke Regional Park, British Columbia
searchResults.description:
This trail begins from the Aylard Farm Trailhead, which can be accessed by following Becher Bay Road just off of East Sooke Road. Light easy trail with nice ocean views throughout and fresh ocean breeze with access to a sandy beach. 

Visit the multiple viewpoints on this trail such as Beechey Head, Squeaky Point and Alldridge Point. Historic petroglyphs can be viewed at Alldridge Point. There are lots of roots and rocks that make travel uneven but not difficult. 

The return trail on the...

searchResults.name: Moments in Time Trail
searchResults.description: This self-guided Nature Trail begins at Lake Crescent Lodge and is a flat 0.6 mile (1km) loop through lakeside forest. Numerous trail-side signs tell the story of Lake Crescent's natural and cultural history. With gorgeous views and plenty for the kids to see, this quick loop has something for the whole family.

searchResults.name: Ranger Hole Trail
searchResults.description: The hike itself isn't difficult, but if you want to get down to the water, you either have to jump from one of the overlooking rocks straight in (we do not advise this), or climb down a steep embankment.

searchResults.name: Rocky Brook Falls
searchResults.description:
Part of a large hydroelectric facility, this area has very strict access, it is recommended to stay on the trail during your visit. 

This gorgeous falls is only a short walk from the road, and is many locals' favorite falls. To find the trailhead, cross the street directly across from the small parking lot. The trail starts beside the concrete building.

searchResults.name: Myrtle Falls Viewpoint via Skyline Trail
searchResults.description: Myrtle Falls can be accessed from the Paradise parking area via the Skyline Trail or Golden Gate Trail. This paved asphalt trail starts with a short uphill trek before climbing a set of stairs to the viewpoint of the 60-foot waterfall. Visitors will likely enjoy the view of Mount Rainier in the background of the falls’ braided cascade. In winter, make sure you come prepared, as the trail can be icy and snow-packed. It is recommended to have trekking poles and micro spikes to be on the safe...

searchResults.name: Camano Island State Park Trail
searchResults.description:
To start, hike up the road that runs along the crest of a bluff. Enjoy views of the ocean and the snow-capped Olympic Mountains from this lofty viewpoint, framed by madrona tree branches.

There are some steps on the hike. After crossing a bridge, you'll enter a marshy area from the edge of the woods, where you might see flocks of little songbirds.

You'll enjoy some fantastic beach walking as you go. You may wander past the picnic tables along the rocky coastline while watching for eagles...

searchResults.name: Foster Island Trail
searchResults.description:
This area is great for walking, running, and birdwatching, with gorgeous scenery and lake views. The trail combines metal walkways, boardwalks, and gravel trails through a wooded area and along the waterfront of Union Bay and the Montlake Cut. 

Some sections can become very muddy and even underwater in a few spots, so come prepared to get your feet wet. Or save this one for the hotter months when it's more likely to have dried up.

searchResults.name: Cave Hole, Fred's Railroad, Quarry, Indian and Red Town Loop
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description:
Gray squirrels, juncos, creepers, and finches are common wildlife sightings at the loop. You'll come across various fungi and gorgeous wildflowers throughout the trail.

The trail winds through a swampy, muddy area. There are some gentle ascents and descents. The centerpiece of the loop is the Cave Hole, which takes you to exciting relics from earlier mining operations and gives you a window into the region's past.

searchResults.name: Panorama Point via Skyline Trail
searchResults.description: This is a popular trail year-round and follows the Skyline Trail to Panorama Point and features breathtaking views of Mount Rainier and the surrounding mountains. In the winter, the road to the trailhead is usually closed, meaning you will have to add a few more to this hike by snowshoeing or cross-country skiing along the road.

searchResults.name: Boulder River
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Pinnacle Peak Full Loop
searchResults.description: This loop starts and ends at the Southern Trailhead parking lot and takes you to Pinnacle Peak. The area is mostly wooded, but there are a few viewpoints along the way offering views of the valley and Mount Rainier. Be prepared for technical sections with steep parts, rock scrambles, switchbacks, roots, and several water crossings. Downloading offline maps is recommended.

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Boulder Garden Loop Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: This loop follows the Boulder Garden and Little Si Trails up and down the side of Mount Si. The area is very popular, so an early start is recommended to get a parking spot on the weekends. Please remain on the established path to help protect the surrounding natural areas. There are some steep sections, some hikers will choose to bring trekking poles along.

searchResults.name: De Leo Wall Trail
searchResults.location_label: Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, Washington
searchResults.description: Most of the hike to De Leo Wall in Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park is easy, with a couple of tough climbing sections. The trail is surprisingly remote given its proximity to civilization and the views from De Leo Wall through the tops of madrone trees are amazing. The Cougar Mountains trail system is complex and although the trails are well-signed, downloading the map ahead of time is a good idea.

searchResults.name: Kanaskat-Palmer Loop
searchResults.description: Beautifully wooded park on the Green River. Miles of trails to explore. Nice camping and picnic areas. 2.4 mile loop hike, with an elevation change of about 218 feet.

searchResults.name: Skate Creek Trail
searchResults.description:
This is a beautiful forest trail with lovely creek views located close to the town of Packwood. The trail meanders alongside the creek for the first half before looping back around to the trailhead on Craig Road.

The trail is relatively easy, with a very slight descent for the first half and ascent for the remainder. There are several offshoots in the area, so it's a good idea to keep an eye on the map to stay on track.

searchResults.name: Palisades Trail (#1198)
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This trail has it all, from beautiful forests, good climbing, and fun descents to technical sections with views of Mt. Rainier from cliffs that will inspire you. Start hiking through old-growth timber. At a tenth of a mile, cross Dalles Creek and for the next mile, be careful as you hike through a series of short switchbacks in loose rock.

searchResults.name: Peabody Creek Trail
searchResults.description: Peabody creek trail has a half mile loop at the bottom, but it connects to a three mile out and back that ends on Hurricane Ridge road. From there the hiker can either return the way they came or hike down the road.  This trail follows and crosses Peabody Creek. The trail is very shaded and provides an escape from the heat.

searchResults.name: Colchuck Lake via Stuart Lake and Colchuck Lake Trail
searchResults.description:
This is a challenging hike with beautiful scenery in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness Area of Washington State. This alpine lake is accompanied by the twin spires of Dragontail Peak and Colchuck Peak at the far end of the lake.

Colchuck Lake Trail starts at Stuart Lake trailhead off of Forest Service Road 7601, which can be accessed from Icicle Creek Road. The parking area can be busy, as visitors access the Enchantments and Stuart Lake from this trailhead. You make need to park a considerable...

searchResults.name: Carter Falls and Madcap Falls via Longmire
searchResults.description: This route is a popular winter snowshoeing and hiking route. This is a great alternative in the winter when the gate is closed in Longmire and you cannot drive further up the mountain. Follow the Wonderland Trail along the Nisqually River to two beautiful waterfalls. There are incredible views of Mount Rainier along this route.

searchResults.name: Greenwater Lakes Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
The trail travels up the valley to two lakes. There are several log bridges that  are in good condition and easy to use with care.

There are two parking areas, one paved parking area for 20 cars, and one that has 10 horse trailer spaces. A vault toilet, bench, and picnic table are available at the paved parking area. If you are camping/backpacking, park in the gravel parking area.

searchResults.name: Rattlesnake Mountain Trail to East Peak
searchResults.description: The Rattlesnake Mountain Trail is a long, continuous climb up to an awesome overlook. From this point, you will be looking back towards North Bend and across the valley at Mount Si. Some stretches of the trail pass through areas that have been logged in recent years, other parts of the route are densely wooded.

searchResults.name: Lighthouse Point and Lottie Point Loop Trail
searchResults.description:
Begin by hiking along Bowman Bay before travelling along Lottie Bay and arriving at Lottie Point. From this point, you can see Pass Island and the Canoe Pass and Deception Pass Bridges.

You will retrace your steps back towards Bowman Bay, then start following the Lighthouse Point Loop. There are more views of this rugged coastline along this loop. Be aware of steep sections and unstable edges along the coast.

searchResults.name: North Beach Trail
searchResults.description:
This beautiful trail follows the northern coastline of Deception Pass State Park. Along the way, you will encounter many interesting rocks and stunning waterfront views. However, you will also need to navigate a few tree roots, so watch your step. 

The trail begins from the Scenic Vista parking lot on State Route 20 and follows the clearly marked North Beach Trail along the length of North Beach and back again.

searchResults.name: Rainier Trail
searchResults.description:
The trail is paved and inside a quiet town with the faraway misty mountains as the background. The trail is good for all ages with a few interesting sites along the way. Several road crossings are necessary to complete this trail, so please use caution. 

Accessibility: There are at least 2 designated accessible spaces in the paved parking lot off of Northwest Gilman Boulevard at the north end of the trail. Both of them are van-accessible with striped access aisles. The trail surface is paved...

searchResults.name: Olympic Hot Springs Trail
searchResults.description:
Open for pedestrians, bicycles, and dogs on leash. Madison Falls parking area is open, parking is limited (trail has been changed to reflect this route. The first approx. 9 miles are paved and can be biked.)

A short, fairly easy hike through moss covered trees leads to a series of hot springs scattered throughout the woods. The water is a great temperature, there is camping in the area (with free permits), and there is a chance for a secluded soak depending on which pool you choose to soak in.

searchResults.name: Talapus Lake Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: The road leading to the trail is rough. The trail is well maintained. The trail can get crowded, but arriving early can help you beat the crowds. Overall, this is a quiet and scenic hike. Go in the fall for beautiful fall colors and beautiful photos. The lake is a great spot to stop for lunch before heading back down the way you came.

searchResults.name: 5-Mile Island via Hoh River Trail
searchResults.description: Ready to step into a fairy tale? The Hoh River Trail starts at the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center in Olympic National Park and is an easy stroll through one of the most beautiful temperate rainforests on Earth. The first few miles are mostly flat and follow the Hoh River, whose unique, milky, slate blue color comes from "glacial flour"—rock dust ground by the ice high on Mount Olympus! Look for giant Sitka spruce and western hemlock trees towering over the path, their branches draped in moss....

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Oxbow Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description:
This is a great kid-friendly hike with well-laid gravel, beautiful mountain views, and mossy trees.

The Washington State Department of Natural Resources maintains this trail.
