Equipment
According...

searchResults.name: Lovers Lane, B-Loop, and Sol Duc Nature Trail Loop
searchResults.description: This trail takes you on a tour through a beautiful Pacific rain forest that includes some very cool bridges.

searchResults.name: WA 520 Trail
searchResults.description:
The trail stretches along WA 520 all the way from Redmond to University of Washington across the bridge over Lake Washington. Very popular with bikers and walkers alike, especially in sunny days. You can enjoy the lake view and the views of surrounding remote mountains.

There is a pedestrian crossing on Northup way just North of where the trail crosses. This is an alternate spot to cross at busy times.


Accessibility: There are 10 designated accessible spaces in the paved parking lot off of...

searchResults.area_name: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Mount Teneriffe via Mount Teneriffe Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Si Natural Resources Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description: This is a very well maintained trail to the summit of Mount Teneriffe. The trail provides the option for a longer hike, if you add in the detour to the Teneriffe Falls. The trail is challenging but provides beautiful views along the trail and fantastic views at the summit. Even with cloud cover, the summit is a surreal experience. A fork a few miles from the summit allows you to take a short spur to the summit of Mount Si as an addition, or as a shorter hike.

searchResults.name: Lodge Lake
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Cheese Rock Trail
searchResults.description: This trail takes you to Cheese Rock where you can enjoy the views of the surrounding mountains or check out the unique rock formations that give the area its name. There is also an off-trail variation of this trail to get to Cheese Rock a shorter way. This mapped route takes a gentler but longer route to the formation.

searchResults.name: Marten Lake Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: The route follows the Snoqualmie Lake Trail for about 2.5 miles before turning onto the Marten Lake Trail. The second part is steep and rutted. The lake is beautiful! Well worth the trek. Downloading the map ahead of time is recommended since cell service is limited in the area and the Marten Lake Trail is not always well defined.

searchResults.name: Lake Wenatchee North: Summer Route
searchResults.description: The loop begins in the forest before heading towards the lake. Once you're at the shoreline, there are views of the mountain on either side of the lake. As you get closer to Route 207 the trail heads back into the forest and the trailhead. The trail is well-defined and easy to follow. There is a restroom halfway around the loop.

searchResults.name: Pacific Northwest Trail: Stage 50C - Cape Alava Connector Trail
searchResults.description:
This is the final, or beggining stage of the Pacific Northwest Trail thru-hike. It follows the Capa Alava Trail east or west, through dense coastal rainforest. The trail ends or begins at the ranger station crossing a bridge over the Ozette River.
 
Check the PNT's official site https://www.pnt.org/ for all relevant and important information. Several permits are necessary before hiking and camping along this trail.

searchResults.name: Goose Rock Summit Trail
searchResults.description:
This trail takes you to the summit of Goose Rock (484ft) in Deception Pass State Park. 

It starts from the visitor center near the Deception Pass Bridge and climbs steeply to the summit, offering great views of the water and Deception Island. 

Shade can be found throughout the hike; however, be prepared for no shade at the summit if you want to enjoy a picnic up here before returning back to the trail.

searchResults.name: Packwood Lake Trail
searchResults.description: A beautiful lake and the perfect setting for a picnic. The view as the lake opens is an unexpected feast for the senses. The area is very popular, so expect to see plenty of families and four-legged friends on the trail, especially on the weekends. The hike begins from a large parking area with trash cans and a pit toilet.

searchResults.name: Enchanted Valley Chalet via East Fork Quinault River Trail
searchResults.description: Starting from the S Shore Rd parking lot, the trailhead starts on the E Fork Quinault River Trail. The first section of the hike to Pony Bridge is covered by thick trees without a lot of views. As soon as you climb out of Pony Bridge, the trail exposure opens up to the Quinault River Valley. The trail is in great condition and well-designed to balance elevation gain with long flat stretches thru idyllic valleys. There are few stretches of strenuous climbing and downhill navigation through...

searchResults.name: Big Cedar Tree Trail
searchResults.description: An easy loop trail leads to this forest giant. Even half-fallen, its height and mass are incredible.

searchResults.name: Ancient Groves Nature Trail
searchResults.description: Right off of Sol Duc Hot Springs Rd, this small but lovely loop guides you through old-growth forests in the lowlands. These massive trunks are older than 200 years and many species depend on the forest for their food and protection. There is only around 5% original lowland left which is why it is so important to protect places like these in Olympic National Park.

searchResults.name: South Beach Trail
searchResults.description:
The breathtaking South Beach coastlines are reachable via the South Beach Trail. The trail winds through the vast American Camp prairie, beginning shortly after the historic buildings. Look for animals such as foxes, rabbits, snakes, and eagles flying overhead. 

The trail steadily climbs as you follow it, offering some fantastic views. The Lookout Bench is a noteworthy location that's ideal for pausing to observe the surroundings. The trail descends gently to South Beach, where you'll be...

searchResults.name: Olalla Canyon Ridge
searchResults.description:
Olalla Canyon Ridge rises above the road, offering sweeping views of the Cashmere Canyons and Wenatchee River. This route starts from Olalla Canyon Road and travels south along the singletrack trail and high desert sage scrub. The ridge ends above Peshastin Pinnacles State Park with the option to continue on a trail that descends switchbacks into the park. There is no water or shade along the trail; plan accordingly. 

There is some contention in this area between public lands and private...

searchResults.name: Mount Pilchuck Trail
searchResults.description:
Mount Pilchuck Trail is a challenging hike to an old fire lookout tower at the top of the mountain that offers panoramic views. The trailhead is located within the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest in the North Cascades area of Washington State off of Mountain Loop Highway. The hiking trail itself is in Mount Pilchuck State Park.

The trail is well maintained and there's a fantastic change in scenery as you ascend up the mountain, starting with lush/old-growth forests at the beginning...

searchResults.name: Bandera Mountain Summit
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Follow the Ira Spring Trail uphill for a little over 2.5 miles to a point where there's a sign pointing out Mount Bandera. From this point, you will follow along the ridge towards Little Bandera Mountain. After this, there is a social trail leading to the summit of Bandera Mountain. To summit the mountain, you will need to tackle a steep and rocky incline, so make sure you come prepared with proper footwear. Downloading the map ahead of time is helpful for navigating off-trail.

searchResults.name: Pratt Lake Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: The Pratt Lake Trail is accessible from the Granite Mountain Trailhead along FR 9034. The Pratt Lake Trail winds through the forest for about the first four miles. After this, it opens up, and there are views of Mount Rainier. Soon after this, you will reach Pratt Lake. The final stretch involves walking across exposed, rocky granite talus slopes, so make sure you wear proper footwear. There are some good backcountry camping spots near the lake.

searchResults.name: Mason Lake via Ira Spring Memorial Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
You may need to bring snowshoes to be able to navigate this trail in winter and spring conditions.
 
The trail up to the summit of Bendera Mountain is a great escape from Seattle as it crests into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness of the Mount Baker Snoqualmie national forest. As you work your way up the mountainside make sure to stop and take in the gorgeous views of Mount Rainier. The last 1.5 miles of the trail gain 1800 feet by cutting straight up the mountain on a narrow path (2 feet wide in...

searchResults.name: Snoqualmie Falls Lower Trail
searchResults.description: This is a short walk from the lower parking lot to view the falls. The route starts out on a paved road, then passes a large hydroelectric diversion structure. Beyond that, a set of stairs takes visitors down to a wooden boardwalk that ends at the lower viewpoint.

searchResults.name: Reflection Lake to Narada Falls via Lower Lakes Trail
searchResults.description: Begin at the Reflection Lakes Parking area and follow the Wonderland Trail to the Lower Lakes Trail to the Narada Falls Trail. Enjoy views of the lake, surrounding mountains, lush forests, and waterfalls along the way. This trail is also popular for snowshoeing in the winter, but due to seasonal road closures, you may need to snowshoe to the trailhead.

searchResults.name: Lena Lake Trail to Upper Lena Lake Trail
searchResults.description:
The 3 mi trail to the lower lake is wide, well maintained and easy to moderate. As you approach the lake you see glimpses of it through the trees. Continue on the main trail which parallels the west side of the lake until you come to the upper lake trail. This trail immediately becomes a single track trail and you notice the increase in elevation. 

The upper lakes trail is noticeably more difficult but becomes even more so as you approach Upper Lena Lake. The last hour or so was very...

searchResults.name: Mount Rainier Standard Summit Route
searchResults.description:
Three-day climb via Camp Muir, Ingraham Glacier, and Disappointment Cleaver.

This is one of the standard routes up Mt. Rainier.  You will ascend the Muir Glacier to Camp Muir and spend the 1st night there.  Then you will continue on to the Ingraham Glacier campsite, which is just another 1,000 feet above Muir.  There you will spend one more short night to acclimatize before leaving camp around 2 am in the morning for an early summit bid.  You will ascend Disappointment Cleaver and hopefully...

searchResults.name: Beechey Head via Coast Trail
searchResults.location_label: East Sooke Regional Park, British Columbia
searchResults.description:
This trail begins from the Aylard Farm Trailhead, which can be accessed by following Becher Bay Road just off of East Sooke Road. 

Light easy trail with nice ocean views throughout and fresh ocean breeze with access to a sandy beach. Visit the multiple viewpoints on this trail such as Beechey Head, Creyke Point, Squeaky Point and Alldridge Point. Historic petroglyphs can be viewed at Alldridge Point. 

There are lots of roots and rocks that make travel uneven but not difficult. Definitely a...

searchResults.name: Falls Creek and Quinault Loop Trail
searchResults.description:
The Quinault Loop, known as the Rain Forest Nature Trail, meanders through old-growth conifer forests. This trail offers a chance to take in Quinault Lake's breathtaking scenery. Benches along the trail's edges as it progressively rises in elevation. Beautiful waterfalls can be found once the trail narrows and veers into the forest. 

The trail gets increasingly rocky as it goes on. The surrounding area of Lake Quinault is dominated by tall Sitka spruce and western hemlocks. The mossy trail...

searchResults.name: Mount Townsend Trail
searchResults.description: The road to the trailhead is mostly paved with some gravel spots. There is no cell service on the road to the trailhead. The road is a single track with plenty of spots to pull out and let cars pass. There are big potholes in the paved road but they’re marked pretty clearly with yellow paint. When you finally get to the end of the paved forest service road and take the left to the trailhead it turns to gravel again and this past half a mile or so had the worst potholes of the whole trip. It's...

searchResults.name: Gem Lake via Snow Lake and High Lakes Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This is a popular trailhead, so an early start is recommended on the weekends. You will climb up a series of switchbacks to reach the top of the pass and drop down towards Snow Lake. After you stop and rest by the water, continue up another climb that has some steep rocky sections to reach Gem Lake. There are some spots to pitch tents at both lakes. Use caution on the way back down, as there is some loose rock and the trail can get busy with several other hikers.

searchResults.name: Camp Muir Route via Skyline Trail
searchResults.description: Experience a legendary climb on the Camp Muir Route, a historic path on Mount Rainier. The camp was named after John Muir, the famous naturalist, who was part of the sixth recorded ascent of the mountain in 1888. The route from Paradise via the Skyline Trail to Camp Muir on Mount Rainier is a high-alpine expedition disguised as a day hike. Starting near the Paradise Visitor Center, the trail climbs steadily through sub-alpine meadows and forest before entering the rocky slopes and snowfields...

searchResults.name: Deer Lake Trail
searchResults.description: Make sure to check the conditions of roads and facilities before you visit at the National Park Service's website https://www.nps.gov/olym/planyourvisit/conditions.htm

searchResults.name: McClellan Butte Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Head up to McClellan Butte, a grand peak in the beautiful Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest near North Bend. This adventure takes you through a lush forest filled with massive old-growth trees like cedar and Douglas fir. You'll cross the wide, flat Iron Horse Trail (also known as the John Wayne Trail) before beginning your steep climb. The butte is named after General George B. McClellan, a pioneer who surveyed this area in 1853, looking for a railroad path through the Cascades. You are...

searchResults.name: Upper Big Quilcene Trail via Marmot Pass
searchResults.description: This is a popular and challenging day hike or overnight backpacking trip. The views at the top are jaw-dropping; there are beautiful mountain views in every direction. The trail was well-maintained and easy to follow. Lots of water sources along the way. The last water source is at camp mystery, about 1-2 miles from the top. The first half of the trail is mostly in the woods, but you will be exposed to the sun during most of the second half.

searchResults.name: Lodge Lake Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: The start point is from the PCT Trailhead on the south side of Snoqualmie Pass. From here, you will follow the PCT uphill across the ski hill and into the woods towards Lodge Lake. This trail can get muddy in the fall. Be sure to bring waterproof shoes if you plan on hiking during this time of year! Keep in mind that during ski season no hiking is allowed.

searchResults.name: Quinault Big Sitka Spruce Tree Trail
searchResults.description: This is a popular natural wonder near the shores of Lake Quinault in Olympia National Forest. This is the location of the world's largest known Sitka Spruce.

searchResults.name: Kalaloch 4th Beach Trail
searchResults.description: This is a short and steep coastal trail through the forest which leads to a driftwood bridge as well as Beach 4. Be on the lookout for seals roaming the shoreline and if you like geology, check out the neat stones here weathered by the ocean and formed by piddock clams. The tide pools have all sorts of interesting creatures inhabiting them. You'll want to check the tide charts before heading out on this adventure as the beach will be underwater during high tide.

searchResults.name: Klahhane Ridge via Switchback Trail
searchResults.description:
A steep series of switchbacks reveals panoramic views and connects to other trails on Klahhane Ridge. Epic panoramic views and colorful wildflowers make each switchback worth it.  As you hike higher and higher, the views will only get better. 

In a half mile, you can turn left to hike along the Sunrise Ridge Trail towards Hurricane Ridge or continue up the Switchback Trail to Klahhane Ridge. Once at the top, you can continue hiking to Heather Park (1.6 miles) or Lake Angeles (2.8...

searchResults.name: Beckler Peak East
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Juan de Fuca Marine Trail
searchResults.location_label: Juan de Fuca Provincial Park, British Columbia
searchResults.description:
This trail's unpredictable weather, challenging terrain and ever-changing conditions result in many hikers needing to be rescued from this trail each year. This trail sees a high number of easily avoidable injuries and search and rescue incidents each year.

The Juan de Fuca Marine Trail is a multi-day hike along some of British Columbia’s most pristine and stunning coastal landscape. The route follows the coastline along Vancouver Island, Canada, and takes hikers to numerous grottos, tide...

searchResults.name: Eagle Peak Trail
searchResults.description:
The first two miles of the Eagle Peak trail is a gradual ascent through a covered forest. Hikers will then reach a stream that diverts them to a beautiful open meadow. Afterward, climb up the saddle with a steep and rocky ascent where you will catch incredible views. Use caution while at the summit as it is very exposed and could become dangerous in unpredictable conditions.

The Native American name for Eagle Peak is Sim-layshe, which means Eagle. At the peak, the north faces views of Mount...

searchResults.name: Snow Lakes Trail
searchResults.description:
This is a beautiful but challenging trail that takes you through awe-inspiring mountain scenery to some pristine alpine lakes. In the early summer, look for wildflowers along the trail and wildlife, including mountain goats, on the hillsides. There is not a lot of signage along the trail, so downloading the route beforehand and staying alert helps navigate the hike. 

Wilderness permits are required for all overnight stays in the backcountry. More information on wilderness permits can be...

searchResults.name: Deception Falls Interpretive Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This interpretive trail takes you underneath the highway to a viewing platform of Deception Creek Falls, then continues along Deception Creek to meet the Tyee River. From there, the trail loops through an old-growth forest to return to the parking lot.

searchResults.name: High Rock Lookout Trail
searchResults.description:
There is about a 9 mile stretch of road that is rough and has a lot of potholes before reaching the trailhead.

This is one of the best hikes with some of the best views in Washington! It’s moderate with a steep incline when you are almost to the lookout. It’s pretty rocky so take your time, the view isn’t going anywhere and it’s well worth the incline!

The trail can get covered in snow in the winter months, so please come prepared: poles, spikes, jackets, waterproof pants, and hiking boots...

searchResults.name: Mount Fremont Lookout Trail via Sourdough Ridge Trail
searchResults.description:
The beginning of the trail starts at the ranger station of the Sunrise Visitor Center, with grassy meadows full of wildflowers. Towards the end of the trail, the landscape is mainly rocks with incredible views of Mount Rainier and the surrounding mountains. Throughout the hike, you will pass through different terrain and scenery as well as see lots of different wildlife such as deer, marmots, and mountain goats. 
 
The views from the Mount Fremont fire lookout are certainly some of the best...

searchResults.name: Hidden Lake Trail
searchResults.description: Hidden Lake is a serene body of water with a steep, rocky hillside towering above it. It is a great place to relax, fish, and get some fresh air. The trail begins from the Hidden Lake Trailhead and heads uphill for about 1/2 a mile before it levels out. Anglers should be familiar with WA state fishing regulations.

searchResults.name: Muir Snowfield Ski Tour
searchResults.description:
Skiing the Muir Snowfield on Mt. Rainier

The Muir Snowfield on the south-east flank of Mt. Rainier offers some of the longest ski descents in the Cascades during the winter, spring and early summer.  Starting at Paradise at 5400 feet, backcountry skiers and riders can climb up to Camp Muir at over 10,000 ft and enjoy the broad snowfield as they carve turns down its moderate slopes back to Paradise.  In the winter, the snowfield is often in the clouds on snowy days so pick your weather and...

searchResults.name: Comet Falls via Van Trump Trail
searchResults.description:
This trail offers diverse landscapes with waterfalls, bridges, flowing rivers/ creeks, meadows, and Mount Rainier as a backdrop. The trek to Comet Falls is well-maintained and not too steep. Comet Falls itself is an amazing waterfall that gets more breathtaking the closer you get.

The road to the trailhead can be dangerous in the winter. Parking is on the road to Paradise and space in the lot is limited.

searchResults.name: The Enchantments Traverse
searchResults.description:
Located in the picturesque Alpine Lakes Wilderness, this epic trip through The Enchantments is a bucket list adventure for any outdoor enthusiast in the Pacific Northwest. Wander through soft tundra meadows, glacial-cirque lakes, crystal clear trickling streams, and impossible granite rock formations in the heart of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. It will make you feel like you're in a completely different world.

This route is meant to be completed as an overnight backpacking trip, although...

searchResults.name: Lake Easton
searchResults.description: This trail starts at the Old US Highway 10 parking lot, near the fishing bridge, and follows along the shores of Lake Easton. It's well-maintained, mostly flat, and easy to follow, with plenty of shade along the way. There are picnic tables where you can stop and rest. At the trailhead, you'll find restrooms, a campground, and an RV park, making it a convenient spot for a day trip or an overnight stay.

searchResults.name: Blanca Lake Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
Blanca Lake Trail is a popular mountain trail through the Wild Sky Wilderness and the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. The hike to Blanca Lake offers many fantastic views. On a clear day, visitors will be treated to great views of Glacier Peak and Columbia Peak across the valley.

The highest point of the trail is at Virgin Lake, and then descends to the southern shore of the gorgeous blue lake below. Once you reach Blanca Lake, views of Monte Cristo can be seen. Waterfalls feed the lake from the...

searchResults.name: Narada Falls
searchResults.description: This is a short walk to a viewpoint of Narada Falls. You can view the falls from the upper pullout if you do not wish to do the hike. This is the largest waterfall viewable by car in the park at 150 feet. Architecture in the park such as the bridge was designed in the 1900s. If you are looking to extend your hike, you can continue on the Wonderland Trail to Carter and Madcap Falls.

searchResults.name: Skyline, Glacier Vista, Upper Skyline and Golden Gate Loop
searchResults.description: The Skyline Trail is one of the most popular trails on the southern side of Mount Rainier. The trail climbs a ridge line to Glacier Vista and Panorama Point on a steady incline that is steep and rocky in sections, so proper footwear is recommended, but the effort is worth it as the two viewpoints offer beautiful views of glaciers, Mount Rainier, and the surrounding mountain landscape. These are great spots to stop for a break, take in the scenery, and have a snack. The trail continues along...

searchResults.name: Silver Falls Loop
searchResults.description:
Walk along this forested trail that runs parallel to the Ohanapecosh River and then crosses over via a bridge offering amazing views of Silver Falls. The water appears turquoise due to the minerals and rushes around the canyon's rocky river. This is a great trail for the entire family. The Ohanapecosh campground offers year-long camping options close by.

Do not go into the water near the falls. Slippery rocks and swift currents make going into the water here dangerous.

searchResults.name: Carter and Madcap Falls via Wonderland Trail
searchResults.description: This is a short, family-friendly hike to two waterfalls! The trail follows the Wonderland Trail alongside the Paradise River. The trail is mostly shaded, as it is a lovely walk through a forest. Keep an eye out for interesting fungi along the way. You will reach Carter Falls first, and Madcap Falls is not too far after.

searchResults.name: Olympus Guard Station via Hoh River Trail
searchResults.description: Get ready for a deep dive into one of the most magnificent temperate rainforests on Earth! The journey to the Olympus Guard Station takes you nearly 10 miles into the heart of the Hoh River Valley in Olympic National Park. The trail is often described by hikers as "flat as a pancake" for this section, making it an easy, peaceful stroll through giant, old-growth forest. You will pass enormous Sitka Spruce and Western Hemlock trees, with moss literally dripping from the branches of Big Leaf...

searchResults.name: Putrid Pete's Peak Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This is a steep hike to a high ridge and summit in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. On the way down the trail can be loose and rocky, trekking poles can be useful to help navigate these steep sections. The first two miles are mostly wooded before you get above the treeline and get awesome views of the surrounding area.

searchResults.name: Red Mountain via Old Commonwealth Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Begin from the PCT parking area at Snoqualmie Pass. The trail passes through dense forest and along Commonwealth Creek. Once the trail begins getting especially steep, the views begin to get better. The final stretch of trail leading to the summit is rocky and involves some scrambling. Hikers who are not comfortable moving over loose, rocky terrain should not attempt this hike. There are awesome views of the surrounding Cascade Range mountains from the top.

searchResults.name: Naches Peak Loop Trail
searchResults.description:
If you’re looking for one of the best hikes in Mount Rainier National Park that is family-friendly and not too long, then the Naches Loop Trail is for you. The trailhead begins at the parking lot by the Stephen Tyng Mather Memorial on the east side of Mount Rainier. The trail follows in a circle around the side of Naches Peak until you loop back to the east side of Naches Peak again. 

Park at Tipsoo Lake, .5 mile west of Chinook Pass on SR 410. For a clockwise hike of the Naches Peak Loop...

searchResults.name: Goat Lake Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
This nice trail is very far into the woods but has beautiful views of N. Cadet Peak and other nearby mountains. There is a parking area by the trailhead but it is at the end of a long rugged dirt road to the trailhead with potholes which is periodically gated about 11 miles from the start of the trail. 

You will follow a steady incline and can choose either the Lower or Upper Elliot Trails, both of which have some rocky and rooted sections. The Upper Elliot Trail is an old logging road. It...

searchResults.name: Narada Falls via Lower Lakes Trail
searchResults.description: This trail begins from Paradise and follows the Lower Lakes Trail past Ruby Falls, Washington Cascades, and ends at Narada Falls. There is a restroom along the way. Enjoy this forested walk along the Paradise River and the views of waterfalls and surrounding mountains. If you are looking for a shorter hike, you can begin this hike midway from the Narada Falls Comfort Station.

searchResults.name: Lower Lakes, Narada Falls, and Wonderland Loop
searchResults.description: This short loop begins at Reflection Lakes and takes you past Narada Falls. There is a lot of beautiful scenery packed into this short hike. Keep an eye out for wildlife along the way and for wildflowers lining the trail in the early summer. This is a great loop for the entire family.

searchResults.name: Cirque Rim Nature Trail
searchResults.description:
With plenty of parking at the trailhead, this route follows a paved trail with a gentile grade.  The overlook provides a nice view of Port Angeles.  This is a great warm-up route before heading out on the other routes from this trailhead.   Head to the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center located in the parking lot for restrooms and more information on the park. 

Accessibility: This trail is likely accessible with assistance for visitors using wheelchairs, mobility equipment, or strollers or...

searchResults.name: Carter, Madcap, and Narada Falls via Wonderland Trail
searchResults.description: This trail follows a section of the Wonderland trail through an old-growth forest along the Paradise River and features three waterfalls. You will reach Carter Falls first and Madcap Falls is not too far away. Continue on past Paradise River Campy to Narada Falls. There is a restroom not far past Narada Falls.

searchResults.name: Hoh River Trail to Blue Glacier Trail
searchResults.description:
This marvelous trail winds through a unique ecosystem. It starts at the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Centre, where parking and restrooms are available. From here, the route follows a relatively flat trail that travels alongside the river.  

Once at 12.4 Miles Camp, the gradient shifts dramatically, and you'll find yourself heading sharply uphill all the way to the top. This hike features some rough terrain traversed with rock scrambling at some points. The scenery is worth the effort as the Blue...

searchResults.name: Mount Angeles via Hurricane Ridge Trail
searchResults.description:
Do not attempt to summit Mt. Angeles without proper equipment and experience.  Scrambling and route-finding skills are needed to access the summit.

After fork from ridge trail, trail steepens. Good stamina required. As you approach cliff, loose scree makes it tougher. Keeping left is important. Avoid the temptation to go straight up. As you get closer, becomes steep 3rd class. Should not be attempted without proper boots. The last pitch is pushing the definition of 3rd class, as there is...

searchResults.name: Snoqualmie Mountain
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: The route to the summit of Snoqualmie Mountain, accessed from the Alpental parking area near Snoqualmie Pass, offers a short but intense alpine climb that demands your full attention. Starting on forested slopes just above the ski resort, the trail soon leaves comfort behind, pushing into steep switchbacks, loose scree, and exposed rock as it heads toward Cave Ridge and ultimately the open summit terrain. Footing is often unstable, the terrain is steep, and the exposure on the final ridge...

searchResults.name: Mount Defiance and Mason Lake via Ira Spring Memorial Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
This route takes you to both Mason Lake and the summit of Mount Defiance. You'll begin by hiking along the Ira Spring Memorial Trail from the Ira Springs Trailhead. You'll also hike on the Mount Defiance Ridge Trail on this trip. There are designated backcountry campsites and a backcountry toilet at Mason Lake. 

The trail can be dusty, steep, and rocky in places, so make sure you come prepared with proper footwear. The last little bit to the summit of Mount Defiance requires a scramble.

searchResults.name: Surprise Creek Trail to Surprise and Glacier Lakes
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: You will walk a short distance up a forest road to access Surprise Creek Trail. You will hike up the valley until the trail joins the Pacific Crest Trail near Surprise Lake. Continue along Surprise Creek until it joins the PCT a second time and passes Glacier Lake. Glacier Lake is probably considered the prettier of the two lakes.

searchResults.name: Nada Lake via Snow Lakes Trail
searchResults.description: The Enchantments is one of Washington's most gorgeous and popular backcountry areas. This route starts at the Snow Lakes Trailhead and follows the trail south over Icicle Creek. It steadily climbs switchbacks before heading down the valley and ending at Nada Lake, which has a few primitive camp spots. This area is on a strict permit system that rangers will regulate.

searchResults.name: Trout Lake via West Fork Foss Lakes Trail
searchResults.description: This trail gets you to a beautiful lake! A permit is required for overnight camping. It is recommended to drive an AWD or high-clearance 4WD vehicle to access this trailhead. If you don't have a 4WD vehicle, you can park further away from the trailhead and walk the rest of the distance, keep in mind this will be increasing the length of your trip.

searchResults.name: Kendall Katwalk Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This is a popular section of the Pacific Crest Trail that follows along the Kendall Katwalk, which is a section of the trail on the side of cliff, with dramatic drop offs and views. On a clear day, you will have great views of Mt. Rainer, Snoqualmie Ski area, peaks, and ranges all around. The trail is well-maintained and easy to follow. The lake at the end is a great spot to stop for lunch or camp if you are doing an overnight backpacking trip.

searchResults.name: Icicle Gorge Trail
searchResults.description:
The lot closest to the trailhead requires a permit (Discover Pass is not accepted) or a fee. The fee envelopes are at the information sign a bit past the parking lot. The road to the trailhead is not paved.

This is a gentle hike, easily enjoyed by both kids and adults, with a low elevation gain, fun bridges, chipmunks, butterflies, and water to observe. There are a few swimming holes and lots of spots for photos along the way. The loop is less than 5 miles long with no side trails to cut...

searchResults.name: Monte Cristo Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: The Monte Cristo Trail begins from the Barlow Pass Trailhead and follows an old railroad grade to the site of an old mining claim. There are a number of backcountry campsites to stay at overnight along the way and the trail parallels the South Fork of the Sauk River for long stretches. As you head up the valley there are views the the mountains towering above you.

searchResults.name: Trout Lake, Copper Lake, Lake Malachite
searchResults.description: This is a perfect hike for those who like to cool off in alpine lakes. The first lake you will pass is Trout Lake, after this you will begin hiking up a series of swithbacks and pass some waterfalls. At the top you can visit Copper and Malachite Lake, which are very close to each other. A permit required for overnight camping.

searchResults.name: Skyline and Alta Vista Trail
searchResults.description: This trail is short and steep, but the views are worth the effort. From the Alta Vista viewpoint, enjoy beautiful views are Mount Rainier and the surrounding mountains. Keep an eye out for wildlife along this trail, including marmots and deer. This is a busy trail, so going in the off-season is a good option if you are looking for more solitude. This trail is also popular for snowshoeing in the winter.

searchResults.name: Swauk Forest Discovery Trail
searchResults.description: Interpretive signs are in place along the trail highlighting the different types of trees you will see along the way. During the fall it is a great hike to see colorful larches. The parking area is a short distance off US 97 near Blewett Pass on Forest Service Road 9716. There is a large sign along the road marking the trailhead.

searchResults.name: Sunrise View Point via High Ridge Nature Trail
searchResults.description:
This trail is a quick climb on a well maintained trail. The viewpoint provides great views of British Columbia, the water and the surrounding mountains. This trail has a great payoff for how easy of a hike it is. Beautiful views, deer, and marmot.

Hurricane Ridge Road is subject to seasonal closure during the winter. For more information on current status, please see https://www.nps.gov/olym/planyourvisit/conditions.htm

searchResults.name: High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin Loop
searchResults.description:
High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin Loop is a popular multi-day backpacking trip. With Sol Duc Falls, Heart Lake and views of Mount Olympus, Blue Glacier, Hoh River and the Seven Lakes Basin— this hike is truly awe inspiring. Expect to come across local wildlife such as black bears. Most people choose to do this hike counterclockwise, but it can be done either way. 

Olympic National Park provides a limited number of permits for overnight campers. Without advanced planning, obtaining a...

searchResults.name: Paradise Glacier Trail
searchResults.description:
Travel through a series of trails interconnecting the subalpine meadows of Paradise. Many sights can be seen of Mt Rainier, Mount Adams, Mount St. Helens, and the Cascade Range. 

Make sure to check the conditions before heading out the door and stay on the trail as to not disturb the subalpine vegetation.

searchResults.name: Royal Basin and Royal Lake
searchResults.description:
The Royal Basin and Royal Lake trail features sections that shift between mild and steep. Log crossings take you to the Meadows campground. There is a stream and sections of the boardwalk here.

The trail follows Royal Creek, meandering through a small valley and crossing a creek. As you ascend, where Royal Creek continues its breathtaking cascades through the forest, the trail becomes steep. Situated just above the meadow lies Royal Lake. After an ascent through the forest, you will emerge...

searchResults.name: Clara Lake and Marion Lake
searchResults.description: The trailhead is located at the entrance to the parking area for Mission Ridge Ski Resort. From here, you will follow the trail uphill through stands of pine trees. You will enter a meadow just before arriving at Clara Lake. Continue along the trail to reach Marion Lake. This is a good spot to see larches change color during October.

searchResults.name: Skookum Falls
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Mount Dickerman Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This loop begins in the forest and eventually breaks out of the trees the higher you get. Expect a continuous climb from the parking area until you reach the summit. There are stunning views along the ridgeline that head towards the top. From here you will have 360-degree views of the surrounding mountains.

searchResults.name: Mini Loop Trail
searchResults.description:
The Mini Rain Forest Trail is a busy trail through lush Washington rainforest that's perfect for the whole family. Truly amazing flora with the huge old trees, mosses, lichens, and ferns. An enchanting place. Check out the exhibits of the temperate rain forest in the Visitor Center.  The Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center is closed in January and February.

The National Park Service maintains this trail.

Accessibility: 

Equipment
Visitors using wheelchairs, mobility equipment, or strollers may...

searchResults.name: Camp Summerland and Lakes via Wonderland Trail
searchResults.description:
This trail follows the Wonderland Trail to Camp Summerland, a popular backcountry camping area. Stop here or continue a bit further to some gorgeous lakes. There are seasonal waterfalls and wildflowers along the trail in the early summer. Do this as a day hike, or spend the night at Camp Summerland for a night under the stars.

This is one of Mount Rainier National Park's many backpacking routes. A wilderness permit is required for all overnight stays in the backcountry. A climbing permit is...

searchResults.name: Mount Ellinor via Upper Trailhead
searchResults.description: This is a steep and challenging climb to the top of Mount Ellinor. At the summit, your efforts are rewarded with beautiful panoramic views. From the top you can see views of Mount Rainier as well as the Olympics. There is little shade in the beginning, so come prepared with sun protection and plenty of water. The final climb to the summit is steep and rocky. Trekking poles are recommended.

searchResults.name: Beckler Peak Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
Begin from the Jennifer Dunn Trailhead and head into the dense forest. You will pass some small cascading streams as you make your way uphill. Near the 1.5-mile mark, you will get your first view of the surrounding mountains. A series of switchbacks and some well-crafted stone steps lead to the summit.

The road to the trailhead is rough and high-clearance vehicles are recommended.

searchResults.name: Cascade Pass Trail
searchResults.description:
Follow the Cascade River Road from Marblemount for 23 miles to the trailhead. The road is paved initially and then becomes gravel, with some large potholes and narrow and steep at the end, so a high-clearance vehicle is needed to reach it. The Cascade Pass parking lot typically opens by the end of June or July.

This is the most popular trail in the national park and can be pretty crowded on weekends. Dogs are not allowed.

searchResults.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie River
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Lake Valhalla via Pacific Crest Trail
searchResults.description: This route follows the Pacific Crest Trail north from Stevens Pass into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. The PCT is a highly trafficked trail and easy to follow, a short spur trail leads to the lake. Lake Valhalla is pristine and Lichtenberg Mountain looms over it. There is a sandy beach that is perfect to relax at.

searchResults.name: Paradise Glacier Caves via Skyline Trail Spur
searchResults.description:
This trail takes you along Mazama Ridge and to the base of Paradise Glacier on Mount Rainier. Begin by following the Skyline Trail, past Myrtle Falls and Sluiskin Falls. From here, join the Paradise Glacier Trail to the base of the glacier.

An interesting landmark at the base of the glacier is an area called "the oven", which is a natural bowl, and due to the reflective effect of the snow on all sides on sunny days, it is a warm, often windless slope even on the coldest clear days.

searchResults.name: Perry Creek Falls via Perry Creek Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: The Perry Creek Trail travels through the forest with occasional glimpses of the surrounding towering peaks. After about a mile the trail begins to climb uphill and crosses several smaller streams that flow into Perry Creek. Perry Falls is a great place to stop and relax before retracing the route back down.

searchResults.name: Mount Baldy via Domerie Divide Trail
searchResults.description: This trail is a steep climb, followed by a scenic walk along the side of a mountain ridge to the summit of Mount Baldy. Trekking poles are recommended to help navigate the steep and rocky terrain. Go on a clear day for the best views. There are beautiful views of Lake Kachess and Lake Easton, Mount Rainier, Glacier Peak, and the Enchantments.

searchResults.name: Lake Ingalls via Ingalls Way Trail
searchResults.description:
There is a small parking lot at the trailhead for the Ingalls Way Trail, and it can fill up quickly in the summer as this is one of the more popular hikes in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Some parking may be allowed along the road, but please do not park on both sides of the road as this blocks emergency vehicle access. 

The first half of the hike is pretty easy, the elevation gain is gradual, and the trail is in good condition.  Just under half a mile into the trail you will come to a...

searchResults.name: Deception Falls
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Margaret Lake Trail
searchResults.description: The ascent to the lake is steep but the views once there are stunning. Bringing waterproof shoes is a good idea. The road to the trailhead is difficult to navigate without a 4x4 vehicle when there is snow/ice. Cars with normal clearance will need to park further down the road, which will add about 2 miles of additional mileage to your hike from the next nearest parking. Downloading offline maps is recommended.

searchResults.area_name: Morning Star Natural Resource Conservation Area
searchResults.name: Greider Lakes Trail
searchResults.location_label: Morning Star Natural Resource Conservation Area, Washington
searchResults.description:
The first 2 miles are along an old gravel road turned trail, mostly flat. After this, you reach the old trailhead and then it’s roughly another 2 miles to the first lake. It will be another 1/2 mile to reach the larger lake. The lakes are a nice place to camp.

While parking is free, registration is required at the kiosk at Olney Pass; where the trails split at the top of the road. Spada Lake is a water reservoir and swimming is not allowed.

searchResults.name: Skyline and Golden Gate Loop
searchResults.description: This loop follows two popular trails in Mount Rainier National Park. Begin by hiking up the Skyline Trail to Myrtle Falls, then connect with the Golden Gates Trail to Golden Gates Falls. Rejoin the Skyline Trail and follow it as it loops back to the trailhead. This route features beautiful views of Mount Rainier and the surrounding landscape. There are some steep sections that can be snow-covered, so make sure to come prepared.

searchResults.name: Rachel and Rampart Lakes Trail
searchResults.description:
The beginning of the trail can be tricky due to the switchbacks. It is very easy to miss turns and end up walking on an old abandoned forest road. Downloading offline maps can help you navigate this trail. The trail is a challenging journey with a lot of elevation gain, and the path is known for its steep, rocky sections. Be prepared for a challenge, and wear sturdy hiking boots to help with the rugged terrain.

Rachel Lake is serene and even more beautiful from the vantage up the trail...

searchResults.name: Burroughs Mountain Loop Trail
searchResults.description:
This trail has great views of Mount Rainier, especially from the second vista. It is mostly a sandy trail but there are rocky sections. You will pass two lakes along the way: Frozen Lake and Shadow Lake. Keep an eye out for wildlife such as mountain goats, pika, and black bears. There is not a lot of shade so be sure to bring sunscreen and water. You can also camp at Sunrise Camp on the south side of the loop.

This is one of Mount Rainier National Park's many backpacking routes. A wilderness...

searchResults.name: Eightmile Lake Trail
searchResults.description: This is a beautiful and popular trail that takes you to an alpine lake. It is a steady climb all the way to Eightmile Lake. It is a little overgrown in some places, and then it opens up into beautiful meadows. There is little shade along the way, so come prepared with sun protection and plenty of water. There are great views of Dragontail to the left in the beginning. Keep an eye out for wildflowers blooming in the spring and early summer.

searchResults.name: Lake Valhalla Trail
searchResults.description: This trail takes you to a beautiful alpine lake. The trail is steep in the beginning, but becomes more gradual as you get closer to the lake. Bring your swimsuit and a lunch and spend the afternoon taking in the scenery and enjoying the lake. The mosquitoes are known to be bad in the early summer, so bring bug spray.

searchResults.name: Pete Lake
searchResults.description: Although mostly easy, this trail is long and does have some slight elevation changes. The trail is mostly shaded through a thick forest. This is a great hike for a hot day. The lake and mountain views are impressive. This is a popular trail for hikers and horseback riders. Be aware of others and share the trail. Pull to the side to let horses pass and put dogs on leash.

searchResults.name: Lake Stuart Trail
searchResults.description: A much quieter alternative to Colchuck Lake on a busy weekend - this trail features a quiet lake with stunning views of the surrounding peaks. Alternately, if you’re trying to experience a little bit of the enchantments and want to up your odds of getting a permit in the lottery Stuart Lake might be perfect for you as well!

searchResults.name: Skyline, Mazama Ridge, Wonderland and Lower Lakes Trail Loop
searchResults.description:
This trail begins by following the Skyline Ridge Trail to the Mazama Ridge Trail to the top of  Faraway Rock. Descend down to the Wonderland Trail and Reflection Lakes, before returning back to the trailhead.

Enjoy beautiful mountain views, meadows, lakes, and a waterfall. There are beautiful and vibrant colors in the fall. Keep an eye out for wildlife along the way.

This trailhead is very popular, so plan to arrive early, especially on summer weekends.

searchResults.name: Vesper Peak Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Vesper Peak towers above the Mountain Loop Highway corridor in the Mount Baker–Snoqualmie National Forest, offering a dramatic alpine summit experience for well-prepared hikers. Starting from the Sunrise Mine trailhead, you’ll ascend through forested terrain, cross creeks, and switch-back up steep alpine slopes until you emerge into open granite slabs and boulder fields. The final push involves scrambling over rock and navigating cairns through talus to reach the 6,214-ft summit. With little...

searchResults.name: Sourdough Gap via Pacific Crest Trail
searchResults.description:
This trail takes you through forest to an alpine lake and provides great views of Mt. Adams, Hood, St Helen’s and Rainier.

Dogs aren’t allowed past Sourdough Gap as the trail enters the National Park and pets are not allowed past that point. You can take them on the trail to the boundary but you wouldn’t be able to go all the way to Crystal Lake. However, this isn't the best trail for dogs as it is rocky and hot.

searchResults.name: Bench and Snow Lakes Trail
searchResults.description:
The Bench and Snow Lake Trail is a great hike for beginners, families with children, or those just looking for beautiful scenery.

“The Bench” is a relatively flat, shelf-like landform on the west side of Stevens Canyon created by a lava flow that erupted about 91,000 years ago. The first part of the trail climbs up to The Bench, through patches of subalpine meadow and huckleberry shrubs to a short spur trail to reach Bench Lake. Continue on the main trail, with sections of steeper log steps,...

searchResults.name: Iron Bear Trail #1351 to Teanaway Ridge Trail #1363
searchResults.description: This is a steady climb to the top of Iron Bear. The trail winds in and out of the forest and open areas with views. Wildflowers can be spotted in these open areas during the early to mid-summer months. From Iron Bear, there is a rewarding view of the surrounding area. The last few hundred yards of the road are often rough, so you may need to park further down the road.

searchResults.name: Mildred Point and Comet Falls via Van Trump Trail
searchResults.description: This trail offers diverse landscapes with waterfalls, bridges, flowing rivers/ creeks, meadows, and Mount Rainier as a backdrop. The trek to Comet Falls is well-maintained and not too steep. Comet Falls itself is an amazing waterfall that gets more breathtaking the closer you get. From there, climb some steep switchbacks up to Mildred Point. This section of trail after Comet Falls is less-maintained and can sometimes be difficult to navigate. Downloading offline maps can help you navigate...

searchResults.name: Thorp Mountain Trail
searchResults.description: Travel through the valley with Thorp Creek running through it before traveling up in the direction towards Thorp Lake. As you ascend higher, the lake will come into view below. At the summit, there is a lookout tower that offers views of Little Kachess Lake, Mount Rainier, and the surrounding Alpine Lakes Wilderness.

searchResults.name: Tatoosh Ridge Trail
searchResults.description: This hike is a severely strenuous challenge, gaining nearly 3,000 to 4,000 feet of elevation over its short length. The trail is relentlessly steep, rarely letting up until you reach the high ridgeline, which makes for a brutal descent. The entire route is highly exposed and often passes over rocky and root-laden terrain. This hike is not for beginners. Due to the difficulty of spotting the trail in the high meadows and among the rocks, it is highly recommended to download the route map and...

searchResults.name: Crystal Lakes Trail to Sourdough Gap
searchResults.description:
This trail begins with a forested, shady, steep climb up some switchbacks. Your efforts are rewarded when you Lower Crystal Lake, which is a great spot to stop for a break and a snack. Continue on to Upper Crystal Lake and Sourdough Gap for more beautiful views.

This is one of Mount Rainier National Park's many backpacking routes. A wilderness permit is required for all overnight stays in the backcountry. A climbing permit is required for all travel above 10,000 feet or on glaciers....

searchResults.name: Cascade Pass and Sahale Arm Trail
searchResults.description:
The first several miles of this Cascade Pass and Sahale Arm Trail include relatively easy switchbacks that develop into challenging inclines over dirt, gravel, and loose rock hiking trails close to the summit. Much of the trail is exposed and can get hot, so make sure you bring plenty of water. Since the trail covers diverse terrain, it is recommended to wear sturdy footwear and bring hiking poles to make the steeper areas easier.  

This hike is amazing for nature, animal sightings, and...

searchResults.name: Sheep Lake Trail
searchResults.description: This trail is a short hike to Sheep Lake, where hikers can stay for the day, camp for the night, or continue on to Sourdough Gap. There are plenty of wildflowers and a lake perfect for swimming in the summer. There are also small, unmarked trails branching through the area for those who like to explore a bit more.

searchResults.name: Pinnacle Peak Trail
searchResults.description: Pinnacle Peak Trail is a popular trail that starts to the south of Reflection Lakes. The rocky trail climbs 1,050 feet up several switchbacks through subalpine meadows to a saddle between Pinnacle Peak and Plummer Peak in the Tatoosh Range. The final stretch to summit the peak requires some challenging scrambling, so make sure you come prepared. The trail can have patches of snow lingering well into summer and steep, exposed drop-offs. From the saddle, view Mount Rainier to the north or look...

searchResults.name: Shadow Lake Trail
searchResults.description:
Begin from the Sunrise Visitor Center and follow the Sunrise Rim Trail to the Wonderland Trail. There is a short loop around Shadow Lake. Sunrise Camp is also nearby if you want to turn this hike into a short overnight backpacking trip. Enjoy beautiful mountain views, alpine meadows, and wildflowers in the early summer.

This is one of Mount Rainier National Park's many backpacking routes. A wilderness permit is required for all overnight stays in the backcountry. A climbing permit is...

searchResults.name: Dead Horse Creek and Golden Gate Trail Loop
searchResults.description:
This is a beautiful looped trail that is similar to the famous Skyline Trail, but it's a shorter route that uses the Golden Gate Trail. 

Start from Paradise Inn and go either clockwise or counter-clockwise. You first witness the picturesque Myrtle Falls, walk through gorgeous meadows with wildflowers and the incredible Mount Rainier in the backdrop. After the paved paths, the trail will get drastically more challenging, taking you through some steep switchbacks, up to some rocky cliffs at...

searchResults.name: Frozen Lake via Sourdough Ridge Trail
searchResults.description: Walk along Sourdough Ridge and enjoy panoramic views of Mount Rainier and the surrounding mountain landscape. This trail begins at the Sunrise Visitor Center and follows the Sourdough Ridge Trail to Frozen Lake. There is a short climb in the beginning, but the walk along the ridge is relatively flat and great for families.

searchResults.name: Reflection Lake to Narada Falls via Wonderland Trail
searchResults.description: This trail begins at Reflection Lake and follows the Wonderland Trail to Narada Falls. There are lovely views of the lake, surrounding mountains, and a waterfall. There is a restroom just past Narada Falls. There is a good amount of incline on the way up to the falls, but Narada Falls is a great place to take a break and catch your breath.

searchResults.name: Kelly Butte Trail #1031
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This trip is to an old U.S. Forest Service lookout. The start of the trail is off of Whistler Creek Road. In the summer season to early fall, the lookout is staffed by USFS volunteers and access is available for the public to tour during staffed hours. When USFS volunteers or officials are not present the lookout tower is locked and closed to the public. During the winter months, the shutters are closed and locked. The stunning 360-degree view of Mt. Rainier is the highlight but on a good day...

searchResults.name: Gothic Basin Trail to Foggy Lake
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
Weden Creek (Gothic Basin) Trail #724 starts in Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and traverses into Morningstar National Resources Conservation Area managed by the Washington State Department of Natural Resources. The trail ends at Foggy Lake where experienced mountaineers gain access to climb Del Campo and Gothic Peaks. Camping is allowed in the basin and surrounding area, but campfires are prohibited.

Start at the Barlow Pass Trailhead and pass the metal gate just south of the parking....

searchResults.name: Kendall Peak via Pacific Crest Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
Kendall Peak is fairly accessible from the Pacific Crest Trail and has various routes to the summit with different difficulty levels. The most direct route is up the north ridge, which has off-trail sections and Class 2 scrambling. Prior hiking experience is required for this summit. 

Climb the Pacific Crest Trail for a bit over five miles. A few feet after the tree stump on the side of the PCT, a booth path will steeply climb to the right and make the final summit push. This is where Class...

searchResults.name: Mirror Lake Trail
searchResults.description: You will walk up the forest service road for a few hundred yards to reach the start of the Mirror Lake Trail. This trail heads uphill and passes Cottonwood Lake first. Mirror Lake Trail runs into the Pacific Crest Trail near Mirror Lake. You can follow the PCT south to explore the shore of Mirror Lake.

searchResults.name: Faraway Rock via Skyline and Mazama Ridge Trail
searchResults.description:
Begin by following the Skyline Trail past Myrtle Falls. Join the Mazama Ridge Trail and follow it to the summit of Faraway Rock. Enjoy beautiful views of Mount Rainier and the surrounding landscape.

If you choose to do this route in winter, keep in the that the route is slightly different. Rather than following the Skyline Trail to Myrtle Falls, follow Valley Road to the 4th Crossing Trail and take that to Mazama Ridge. The section of the Skyline Trail near Myrtle Falls can be...

searchResults.name: Cirque Rim to Sunrise View Point Trail
searchResults.description: The Cirque Rim Nature Trail at Hurricane Ridge in Olympic National Park is a fantastic way to see giant mountains and amazing views without a long, hard hike. You’ll journey along the rim of a glacially carved basin, often called a cirque, with views stretching out towards scenic Sunrise Point and across layers of mountain peaks. The trail offers a mix of experiences, beginning with a paved path for a pleasant start, and later transitioning to a natural surface of dirt and rocks as you...

searchResults.name: Mirror Lake via Pacific Crest Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: Mirror Lake via the Pacific Crest Trail offers a scenic trek through the dense forests of the Snoqualmie Pass region. This route traverses a well-maintained section of the historic Pacific Crest Trail, leading hikers past seasonal ponds and through groves of noble fir and mountain hemlock. While the path is generally easy to follow, be prepared for a rocky and rooty tread that requires steady footwork, especially on the descent. The destination is a crystal-clear alpine lake tucked beneath...

searchResults.name: Skyscraper Mountain via Sourdough Ridge and Wonderland Trail
searchResults.description:
This is a challenging, yet rewarding hike. The trail follows Sourdough Ridge to the Wonderland Trail and passes Frozen Lake along the way. This is a great trail for viewing wildlife, including mountain goats, bears, marmots, and more.

The views from the top of Skyscraper Peak are breathtaking - mountains as far as you can see! The top of Mt Rainer looks so close you could touch it, and even a view of the Fremont Fire Lookout across the valley.

searchResults.name: Lake Stuart and Colchuck Lake Trail
searchResults.description:
An inviting lake beneath the fearsome north face of one of Washington's highest and most imposing peaks.

Stuart Lake is at 5600 feet elevation in the Enchantment Mountain range. It is about a 30 acre lake with clear water and easy fishing access in many places. The lake has a very healthy population of gorgeous cutthroat trout.

The trail to the lake is well marked and well used. It follows Mountaineer Creek for over 3 miles, at which time you start getting great views of the Enchantment...

searchResults.name: Marmot Lake and Jade Lake via Deception Pass Trail
searchResults.description: A gorgeous, difficult hike that may require off-trail hiking, steep inclines, and multiple river crossings. Enjoy beautiful views, alpine lakes, and great camping spots. Be prepared to get your feet wet and pass through snow even in summer weather. You can easily fall through snow as it melts. Depending on the season the trail is not easily seen and reaching Jade Lake can be difficult, as noted below. This area is a fragile alpine environment and Leave No Trace principles should be practiced...

searchResults.name: Shriner Peak Lookout Trail
searchResults.description:
The Shriner Peak Trail not only provides incredible views of the park’s eastern wilderness but also challenges hikers with a good workout. The 360-degree panorama from the summit is one of the best in the park.


The wilderness campsites at Shriner Peak are located near the lookout and offer an incomparable view of Mount Rainier at sunrise. Well worth the effort of waking early! 

A spring located about one mile back down the trail is the only source of water for this camp. Treat water before...

searchResults.name: Perry Creek Falls
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Minotaur Lake Trail
searchResults.description: This trail is a popular day hike and overnight backpacking trip. The trail is steep, but your efforts are rewarded with beautiful views! Bring your fishing pole and spend the afternoon fishing at the lake. Be sure to bring bug spray, especially in the early summer, as the mosquitoes tend to be bad on this trail.

searchResults.name: Silver Falls via Laughingwater Trail
searchResults.description: This is an alternative route to Silver Falls that begins from the Laughingwater Trailhead. The trail takes you through a lush forest and opens up to the rushing Ohanapecosh River and the beautiful Silver Falls. The turquoise color of the water in the river comes from minerals and sediments that flow down the river from the glaciers above. Be careful not to go into the water near the falls, as slippery rocks and swift currents make the river dangerous.

searchResults.name: Silver Peak Trail
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This demanding summit trek requires negotiating exposed Class 3 scrambling and navigating fields of shifting rock and scree near the peak. The route begins easily enough along the famed Pacific Crest Trail before quickly turning into a steep, rugged boot path that gains most of the elevation rapidly. Near the summit, hikers must be prepared for a taxing scramble that calls for confident footing and the use of hands. The reward for the climb is an unparalleled 360-degree panorama of the...

searchResults.name: Tipsoo Lake to Dewey Lake Loop
searchResults.description:
A beautiful hike with minimal elevation gain around Naches Peak with an option to visit Dewey Lake.

This is a great trail that is perfect for the family within Rainier National Park.  It will take you from Tipsoo Lake with its great view of Mt. Rainier around Naches Mountain in a loop hike with many spectacular views.  On the opposite side of Naches Peak from the highway you will have the option at a junction to visit two more alpine lakes if you have the energy for the descent down to them...

searchResults.name: Dead Horse Creek Trail
searchResults.description: This is a popular trail that leaves from the Paradise Inn area. The trail is short but steep, and mostly paved. There is little shade along the route, so it is recommended to start early in the morning (this is a great place to catch the sunrise) and bring plenty of water. There are beautiful views of Mount Rainier, glaciers, and the surrounding landscape. There are many nearby side trails and options to turn this into a longer hike or a loop if you are looking for something more challenging.

searchResults.name: Dewey Lake Trail
searchResults.description: This trail goes along the PCT to Dewey lake. Camping is allowed with a self issued wilderness permit at the trailhead. This trail briefly enters Mount Rainier National Park, and dogs are only allowed on the PCT within the park boundaries.

searchResults.name: Burroughs Mountain Trail
searchResults.description:
This trail takes you to the most accessible tundra in the Cascade Range and provides breathtaking views of Mount Rainier and the surrounding mountains. Due to the fragile ecosystem here, please be sure to stay on the trail. This trail follows along a ridge line and provides little shade. Bring sun protection and plenty of water.

This is one of Mount Rainier National Park's many backpacking routes. A wilderness permit is required for all overnight stays in the backcountry. A climbing permit...

searchResults.name: Sahale Arm Trail to Sahale Mountain
searchResults.description: Begin by hiking up a long series of switchbacks to a point overlooking Doubtful Lake. From this point, you hike up the ridge line and arrive at a talus field. The rocky trail leads to a camp at the base of the glacier. The route to the summit crosses the Sahale Glacier to the summit of the mountain. Crossing the glacier should not be attempted without prior glacier travel experience and a healthy knowledge of glacier travel best practices. This is considered one of the most beautiful areas in...

searchResults.name: Sunrise Rim Trail
searchResults.description:
The Sunrise Nature Trail traverses subalpine meadows just north of the Sunrise parking area. A gentle climb to the ridge top offers awesome breathtaking views of Mount Rainier, with Mount Baker, Glacier Peak, and Mount Adams in the distance. Stay on trail to protect fragile plants. Rocky Mountain goats can sometimes be seen along the trail. 

At an elevation of 6,400 feet, Sunrise is the highest point that can be reached by vehicle at Mount Rainier National Park. In summer, mountain meadows...

searchResults.name: Mount Margaret Trail
searchResults.description:
This route takes you along the Mount Margaret Trail to Mount Margaret on a steady incline. The end is steep, and there are some rocky sections, so it's recommended to bring trekking poles. The panoramic views are worth the extra effort. 

The road leading to the trailhead is rocky, it can be difficult without 4WD or high clearance.

Cell reception can be tricky. Downloading the map is recommended, as the trails are not well-marked.

searchResults.name: Emmons Moraine Trail
searchResults.description: The glacier basin trail is a lovely, easy, and well maintained trail. At just under a mile, you reach a fork, and take a left. From there is is a short walk to a log turned into a foot bridge (complete with guard rail) where you cross. After that, a few short switchbacks puts you up on the ridge, and there are a couple of viewpoints just after. You get excellent views of the top of the glacier (it looks like a rock wall due to a debris fall covering it in rocks) and the beautiful, turquoise...

searchResults.name: Mount Catherine Trail #1348
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This is a short but steep hike up to a wonderful viewpoint. As you head uphill through the woods, there are several spots where the mountains come into view. From the top, you can see Mount Rainier and Keechelus Lake. The last section to the summit requires a bit of a scramble and can have a rope to help with the climb. The trail is usually busy on the weekends, so an early start is recommended to beat the crowds.

searchResults.name: Sunrise Rim Trail Loop and Mount Fremont Lookout
searchResults.description:
A loop trail on the northeast side of Mt. Rainier to Burroughs Mountain & Frozen Lake with a side trip to Mt. Freemont 

This is a great loop hike that will take you to a fire tower, several alpine lakes and a close up view of Mt. Rainier from the top of Burroughs Mountain with a return on the famous Wonderland Trail.  The trails are easy to follow and the views are spectacular.  Bring a camera.

This is one of Mount Rainier National Park's many backpacking routes. A wilderness permit is...

searchResults.name: Sunrise Nature Trail
searchResults.description: This trail is a short, family-friendly, self-guided nature trail near the Sunrise Visitor Center. The trail takes you through an alpine meadow and features beautiful views of Mount Rainier and the cascades. Keep an eye out for wildflowers in the early summer. This is a great spot to watch the sunrise. Wildlife is frequently spotted along this trail, including mountain goats and black foxes.

searchResults.name: Frog Mountain Trail
searchResults.description:
This route takes you along Frog Mountain Trail on a steep and well-maintained path with a series of switchbacks that can be challenging. Once you reach the summit of Frog Mountain, you will be rewarded with views of Glacier Peak and Mount Rainier.

Overnight camping is not allowed. A parking permit is not needed, and there is access to a pit toilet near the parking lot.

searchResults.name: High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin
searchResults.description: This loop trail is the best way to experience Olympic National Park in Washington. It is a great backpacking/camping route since there are many campgrounds along the loop. You can enjoy a beautiful hike through the lush forest, along the ridgeline, and past beautiful lakes, taking in the serene surroundings and views of the cascade. The trail is rich in fauna and flora, providing opportunities to spot bears and elks.

searchResults.name: Navaho Peak
searchResults.description:
This trail travels over a high country pass boasting stunning views of the Stuart Range. A high clearance vehicle is highly recommended to make it to this trailhead. 

The summit boasts outstanding views and there are plenty of good spots to tent camp along the way. The trail is mostly wooded for the first 5 miles before it opens up and the views get better.

searchResults.name: Grand Park via Lake Eleanor Trail
searchResults.description:
Park in the parking near the trailhead on Huckleyberry creek road, also called Forest Road 7360.

The hike begins just off FR 7360, following a footpath along the edge of Eleanor Creek. The trail enters a mixed forest and begins a moderate climb toward Lake Eleanor. Within 0.5 miles, you will cross into Mount Rainier National Park. No dogs allowed. Camping is allowed at the lake with a permit.

The FS 7360 will close in mid December each year, there is a gate that closes.
