searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Lower Lakes, Wonderland, Mazama, Skyline, and Dead Horse Creek Loop
searchResults.description: This trail leaves from the popular Paradise Inn. This is a busy trailhead, so be sure to arrive early, especially on summer weekends. Begin by following the Skyline and Dead Horse Creek Trail to Glacier Vista and Panorama Point, two viewpoints providing interesting and beautiful views. Continue along the Skyline Trail to the Mazama Trail. Ascend the Mazama Ridge Trail to the top of Faraway Rock. This is a great vantage point and offers beautiful views on clear days. Descend down to Reflection...

searchResults.name: Berkeley Park Trail
searchResults.description:
Berkeley Park is a lovely meadow alongside Lodi Creek. This trail begins at the Sunrise Visitor Center and follows the Sourdough Ridge Trail to Frozen Lake. From there, follow the Wonderland and Northern Loop Trail to Berkeley Park. Enjoy beautiful views of Mount Rainier and the subalpine landscape.

This is one of Mount Rainier National Park's many backpacking routes. A wilderness permit is required for all overnight stays in the backcountry. A climbing permit is required for all travel...

searchResults.name: Thunder Mountain via Tunnel Creek Trail and PCT
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description:
The first 2 miles are steep up to Hope Lake. The trail is well-maintained but there are rocks and roots throughout, so watch your step. After Hope Lake, you will join the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT). This section up to Trapp Lake has less elevation gain, a nice break from the steep climbing in the beginning. There is a side trail where you can veer off to visit Trap Lake if you wish.

After Trapp Lake, the trail becomes steep again. Make sure to follow your GPS closely as the trail diverges...

searchResults.name: Bench Lake
searchResults.description:
The Bench is a great hike for beginners, families with children, or those just looking for beautiful scenery. It is about 0.75 miles to Bench Lake.

“The Bench” is a relatively flat, shelf-like landform on the west side of Stevens Canyon created by a lava flow that erupted about 91,000 years ago. The first part of the trail climbs up to The Bench, through patches of subalpine meadow and huckleberry shrubs to a short spur trail to reach Bench Lake. 

The trail, especially around Snow Lake, can...

searchResults.name: Lunch Lake Trail
searchResults.description:
This route begins from the parking lot at the end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road and leads to Lunch Lake in Olympic National Park. It’s a beautiful hike through an ancient forest featuring a three-prong waterfall from the Sol Duc River that captures rainbows in the spray. Along the way, you'll encounter spring-fed and snow-runoff creeks, lakes, small ponds, and campsites.

It’s a challenging hike recommended for experienced and well-equipped hikers. Be prepared for a remote area with steep...

searchResults.name: Spectacle Lake
searchResults.description:
Spectacle Lake is truly breathtaking. The first half of the trail is relatively easy. The second half gets gradually harder as you start to head up with less and less coverage. The switchbacks leading up to the lake are steep and challenging with some loose rock, so make sure you save your energy for the last couple of miles. Once you pass that, you will be greeted with a stunning view. 

This is a popular backpacking spot, so it is recommended to arrive at camp early so you can secure a...

searchResults.name: High Lakes Loop Trail
searchResults.description: This trail starts from either end of the parking lots next to Reflection Lakes. Starting from the west side of the lake, the trail climbs up to the ridge above the lake, follows the ridge to Faraway Rock, then descends back to the lake. Faraway Rock overlooks Louise Lake and Stevens Canyon to the east, as well as providing views to the southwest of the Tatoosh Range and Reflection Lakes. The trail is dirt, broken at times by tree roots and rocks. The eastern side of the loop from Faraway Rock...

searchResults.name: Dege Peak via Sunrise Visitor Center
searchResults.description: This trail begins from the Sunrise Visitor Center and takes you to the summit of Dege Peak. The trail is steep in the beginning, but flattens out once you reach Sourdough Ridge. Enjoy breathtaking views of Mount Rainier and the surrounding subalpine landscape along the way. Alternatively, you can hike to the summit of Dege Peak from Sunrise Point.

searchResults.name: Sunrise Ridge Trail to Klahhane Ridge
searchResults.description: Starting at the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center, hike along Sunrise Ridge to gain great panoramic views. After 2.5 miles, you will intersect the Switchback Trail. Travel another mile from there to gain Klahhane Ridge. Further hiking will lead you to Heather Park (1.6 miles) or Lake Angeles (2.8 miles).  Steep elevation gains lead to beautiful views throughout the hike.  The intersection of Klahhane Ridge offers a perfect vantage point to see Mount Angeles and Hurricane Ridge road as well as a...

searchResults.name: Tuck and Robin Lakes
searchResults.description: The Tucquala Meadows Trailhead is a popular access point to the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Hikers should aim for an early start since the trailhead is known to be busy on weekends through the summer months. After hiking up the valley and past Hyas Lake, you will begin to hike uphill, which has some steep and rocky sections, especially at the end, so make sure you wear proper footwear. At the junction with the Robin Lakes Trail, take this towards Tuck and Robin Lakes. This is a popular...

searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Del Campo Peak
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This formidable route to Del Campo Peak requires experience with sustained Class 3 and Class 4 scrambling, a high degree of comfort with exposure, and a safety helmet due to significant rockfall hazards. The approach begins easily along the former mining road before hitting the steep, direct ascent into Gothic Basin—a rugged section constructed by miners that foregoes the usual switchbacks found in the North Cascades. Once past Foggy Lake, the route transforms into a technical scramble over...

searchResults.name: Snow Lake, Gem Lake, Upper Wildcat Lake
searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington
searchResults.description: This well defined trail will lead past four separate lakes, ending at Upper Wildcat Lake. The ice cold waters make this a perfect spot to jump in during the hot summer months. At points you will walk across some talus fields, but there are rock cairns to follow and help you stay on course. An early start is recommended during the summer since the parking area can fill up.

searchResults.name: Plummer Peak via Pinnacle Peak Trail
searchResults.description: Plummer Peak is a great alternative to Pinnacle Peak and is a maintained trail that requires only a small bit of scrambling, but can be steep and slick in some areas. Follow the Pinnacle Peak Trail to the Pinnacle Saddle. From here, the trail is a little exposed; be careful if you are afraid of heights. From there, continue on to the summit of Plummer Peak. Enjoy beautiful panoramic views of Mount Rainier and the surrounding mountains. Be aware that the trail can be very windy at the top, so...

searchResults.name: Mount Townsend via Little Quilcene Trail
searchResults.description:
This route takes you on a challenging incline. Of the multiple approaches up Mount Townsend, this option has the shortest distance with the least elevation gain. The trail is well-maintained, and the top offers some stunning views with plenty of wildflowers along the way. The hardest and steepest part of the trail is at the beginning. 

The trail getting to the trailhead is rough and not well-maintained, so it's best to take your time and download the maps beforehand, as the signal can be weak.

searchResults.name: Dragontail Peak via Stuart Lake Trail
searchResults.description: The route to Dragontail Peak from the Stuart Lake trailhead slices through Washington’s rugged Stuart Range and culminates atop one of its most dramatic granite summits. Beginning with the trail into Colchuck Lake, you’ll traverse forested slopes, lakeside campsites, and eventually the steep talus fields ascending toward Aasgard Pass. From the pass, you enter alpine terrain: snowfields or glacier remnants, depending on the season, and finally talus/slab scrambling to the summit ridge of...

searchResults.name: Little Annapurna via Snow Lakes Trail
searchResults.description: Little Annapurna 2,586m (8,485ft) towers over the Enchantments and offers some of the most dramatic views in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Reaching this granite summit is a major physical undertaking that requires navigating the legendary Aasgard Pass, a steep and punishing mile of loose scree and talus. This route is recommended only for experienced hikers comfortable with high-altitude environments, potential hands-on scrambling, and complex wayfinding across granite slabs. Early season...

searchResults.name: Maiden Peak from Deer Park Campground
searchResults.description:
The hike begins at the Deer Park Trailhead, which provides parking and restrooms. The road to the trailhead is a rough, unpaved road. The trail follows the Obstruction Point-Deer Park Trail around Green Mountain to the summit of Maiden Peak. The first three-quarters of the hike is through the forest, while the last part takes you through meadows with panoramic views of the valley and mountains. 

You'll encounter incredible scenery, including forests, meadows, alpine views, and larger...

searchResults.name: Crystal Lake via Sourdough Gap and Sheep Lake
searchResults.description:
While the majority of this trail is within Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, the trail crosses into Mount Rainier National Forest just before Crystal Lake. Those who are planning to camp overnight at Crystal Lake will be required to obtain a wilderness permit from Mount Rainier National Park. 

Dogs are allowed on the trail until you reach Sourdough Gap, where you will enter the Rainier portion of the trail. Dogs are not allowed there, so if you want to reach Upper Crystal Lake, you'll have...

searchResults.name: Tipsoo Lake Loop
searchResults.description: This is a great, family-friendly hike around Tipsoo Lake. Remember that pets are not allowed around the lake. The snow usually melts by June or July. Keep an eye out for wildflowers in the early summer. There are beautiful mountain views. This is a great trail if you are looking for a quick stop to stretch your legs.

searchResults.name: Sunrise Backcountry Camp Loop
searchResults.description:
Sunrise is the highest elevation that can be reached by vehicle in Mount Rainier National Park. There are breathtaking views of Mount Rainier. This short loop takes you to Sunrise Camp, which is a popular spot for overnight backpacking. This is an easy family-friendly day hike or overnight backpacking trip.

This is one of Mount Rainier National Park's many backpacking routes. A wilderness permit is required for all overnight stays in the backcountry. A climbing permit is required for all...

searchResults.location_label: Mount Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, Washington

searchResults.name: Mount McCausland Trail
searchResults.description:
Starting at the Smithbrook trailhead,  you arrive at a junction with the Pacific Crest Trail after about a mile.

Turn left (southbound) on the PCT on a relatively flat section. About 2 1/2 miles from the trailhead you'll find a turn-off for Mt. McCausland on your right. The trail is unmarked. If you see Lake Valhalla on your left, you have gone too far. The trail to Mount McCausland starts out gentle but the middle section is very steep. You gain 650 feet in about half a mile. There is a...

searchResults.name: Glacier Basin Trail
searchResults.description: Although an effort was made to mine copper ore in this area in the late 1800s, nothing of commercial value was ever extracted and mining efforts were eventually suspended. The trail follows the White River for 3.5 miles. One mile beyond the trailhead is a junction with the Emmons Moraine Trail. This one-mile round-trip spur trail leads to a viewpoint that overlooks the Emmons Glacier, the largest glacier in the 48 contiguous United States. At first, the ascent is gradual but becomes steeper...

searchResults.name: Silver Forest Trail
searchResults.description: Stunning, easy trail with remarkable views of Rainier. Perfect stroll to take after a strenuous hike but you’re not quite ready to wind down for the day. Also a perfect trail for families with children. Do not miss stopping at Emmons Vista along the way, it is one of the best views of Rainier in the park! There is little shade along this trail, so be sure to bring sun protection and water.

searchResults.name: Crystal Peak Trail
searchResults.description: This is a must-do hike for visitors to Mount Rainier National Park. The climb is challenging, but the views are worth your effort. Climb this peak for terrific views of Hood, St. Helens, Chimney Rock, Adams, Glacier Peak and of course the massive frame of Mt. Rainier up the valley. Keep an eye out for wildflowers along the trail in the early summer.

searchResults.name: Faraway Rock via Reflection Lakes
searchResults.description: This trail takes you from Reflection Lakes to the top of Faraway Rock. This is the shortest way to approach Faraway Rock, making it a good option for families. Enjoy beautiful lake views and panoramic views of the surrounding landscape from the top of Faraway Rock. There is a small parking lot at the start.

searchResults.name: Cascade Pass Trail to Doubtful Lake
searchResults.description:
Cascade Pass Trail is arguably one of the park's most beautiful and popular trails. The challenging singletrack trail leads to Cascade Pass, an alpine mountain pass at 5,391 feet, with panoramic views of the North Cascades. This route continues northeast and descends to Doubtful Lake, a scenic alpine lake below Sahala Arm. 

This trailhead will fill up on weekends and holidays. There are two pit toilets at the trailhead.
